articles.summary: Shipping is no stranger to transformation. Changing engines, evolving crewing models and relocating shipbuilding all took costs out of moving cargo by sea. articles.body: USD ≈7bn lost per year: the hidden cost of how shipping trades in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 Shipping is no stranger to transformation. Changing engines, evolving crewing models and relocating shipbuilding all took costs out of moving cargo by sea. Torvald Klaveness believes the next shift is hiding in plain sight, in how cargo owners, operators, shipowners and ports contract and coordinate to harvest value from aligned incentives. Klaveness has now published a study that puts a number on it. From the cargo owner’s perspective, the study identifies and quantifies around USD 7bn a year in potentially avoidable costs across dry bulk and product tanker shipping. The inefficiencies range from vessels waiting to berth and ships that are not loaded to full capacity, to contracts that do not reward efficiency. Klaveness believes the full potential could reach USD 10–20bn a year, or 5–10% of the roughly USD 190bn spent on freight in the two segments. The study reviewed around 50 possible sources of inefficiency and examined 14 in depth, so roughly half of the potential is still to be explored. The USD 7bn is an indicative sum of individual estimates, with some overlap, and is not a savings forecast. It shows the scale of what is at stake. “Improving efficiency in shipping has motivated Torvald Klaveness for 80 years, and we have never achieved it alone,” comments Ernst A. Meyer, CEO of Torvald Klaveness. “That is how shipping has always moved forward. Over the years, we have sensed that significant value is lost every day in how decisions are made across companies. Every party is acting rationally, but the incentives don’t line up. That is the opportunity, and no single company can or should capture it alone.” The portfolio companies in which Torvald Klaveness has active ownership in have worked on aspects of trading efficiency for years, but lacked a clear picture of how big the problem was, or whether long-standing industry norms could realistically change. The study set out to answer both questions. A project team from across the industrial portfolio spent almost four months on it, and an external agency led the work to quantify and verify the results. Ernst Meyer, Torvald Klaveness President and CEO What this means for the industry Klaveness believes pressure and capability are arriving at the same time. Better data, better visibility into cargo flows and vessel movements, and advances in AI make these inefficiencies easier to see and increasingly practical to address. At the same time, supply chains are growing more complex, and expectations on transparency, resilience and emissions are rising. Klaveness will keep building its business in this area and is backing trading efficiency through its innovation and investment strategies. Even so, the opportunity depends on how the whole industry trades, not on any one company. “We could have kept this to ourselves, but it won’t be solved that way,” says Meyer. “The opportunity only gets captured if the industry sees it the same way and starts changing how we trade, and those who are ready will move faster. We intend to be at the front, and we’d like to test what works in practice with the people we trade with.” About the study The study draws on Klaveness’s own voyage data and experience, and open external sources led by Cardo Partners, an independent advisor. A methodology note and further detail on the individual inefficiency drivers are available in the Trading Efficiency Report or on request. articles.title: Peninsula sees bunker market disruptions lasting into 2027
articles.summary: Bunker supplier Peninsula expects the bunker fuel market disruptions to persist into 2027 amid geopolitical conflicts, according to company executives, as the marine fuel supplier expands its barge fleet to navigate volatile markets. articles.body: Peninsula sees bunker market disruptions lasting into 2027 in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 Bunker supplier Peninsula expects the bunker fuel market disruptions to persist into 2027 amid geopolitical conflicts, according to company executives, as the marine fuel supplier expands its barge fleet to navigate volatile markets. The outlook comes after significant market volatility in Singapore, the world’s largest bunker port, for much of 2026, driven by supply disruptions, elevated freight costs and changing arbitrage economics following the outbreak of conflict between the US and Iran in late February. “Our base case is that this disruption will continue over the next six months,” Jonas Bentsen, Peninsula’s head of physical sales, recently told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. “We’re not going to see markets moving back to normal in the short term.” Fuel oil and residues exports from Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports to Singapore fell from 186,000 barrels/day in the first quarter to 22,000 b/d in Q2 before recovering 96,000 b/d in Q3, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data. Bentsen said geopolitical risks would continue to shape the bunker industry, with limited alternative sources of high-sulfur fuel oil supply from the Middle East expected to keep Singapore’s market under pressure. “It’s very tricky to see any viable alternative supply locations from the Middle East into Singapore, specifically for high sulfur,” he said. “And that’s also why we believe that market will remain very tight for some period of time.” Platts assessed the Singapore-delivered 380-centistoke high sulfur fuel oil bunker premium over the corresponding free-on-board Singapore cargo benchmark at $50.12/metric ton on Nov. 23, much higher than the pre-war level of $9.34/mt assessed on Feb. 27 but down from a record high of $228.73/mt on March 10. The front-month Singapore 380 CST HSFO crack against Dubai crude stood at minus $4.643/b on Nov. 23, compared with an all-time high of $14.045/b on March 9 and the recent peak of $12.202/b on Oct. 15, according to Platts assessments. The retreat reflects an easing of immediate supply pressures since the earlier disruption, although uncertainties over the availability and freight costs remain. S&P Global Energy CERA analysts expect HSFO cracks to normalize as bunker demand was fulfilled and freight rates stabilized, although winter power-generation demand could limit the decline, according to the November Asia Refined Products Short-Term Outlook published on Oct. 30. The analysts projected Asian fuel oil production at 1.39 million b/d in Q4, down 37,000 b/d year over year, as refiners continued to prioritize higher-margin middle distillates over residual fuels. CERA analysts also forecast Middle Eastern fuel oil shipments to Singapore at 164,000 b/d in November, compared with 170,000 b/d in October and 175,000 b/d in September. Supply flexibility Against this backdrop, Peninsula is seeking to leverage its global physical supply network and shipping arrangements to respond to changes in regional bunker demand. “It’s about constantly weighing up the arbitrage opportunities and taking advantage of them, and being efficient in terms of where we move products from and how we can move them as economically as possible,” Bentsen said. He said the company’s scale allowed it to reposition bunker barges between markets experiencing different supply and demand conditions. “We are able to move those from different regions and swap them to locations where we see an increase in demand, and away from locations where we see a decrease in demand,” he said. “That helps us and our customers follow the market.” Peninsula sold 20 million mt of marine fuels in 2025, up 11.1% from the previous year, according to the company. The supplier operates more than 50 bunker supply ships, which are owned by Tanker Management and chartered into Peninsula. Like Peninsula, Hercules was founded b John A. Bassadone. One of the largest in the bunker industry, Peninsula’s physical supply operations span locations across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas, alongside reselling activities covering more than 500 ports. Fleet development Peninsula is expanding its access to bunker ships capable of handling alternative fuels as it prepares for changing demand. “We’re now in the process of getting the newbuilds, and that will continue over the next couple of years,” Jeroen De Vos, Peninsula’s global head of operations, told Platts. “It takes time to build. I think there is a business opportunity to expand.” Hercules Tanker Management has a newbuilding program involving 10 IMO Type II chemical tankers of about 7,882 deadweight tons each. Four have been delivered, with Peninsula time-chartering three. Another delivery is expected around March. De Vos said the ships could carry methanol and B100 biofuels, positioning Peninsula for future alternative-fuel demand. “We’re also building a second LNG bunker vessel of 18,000 cubic meters, which will be ready for operation mid-2027,” he said. De Vos said uncertainty over future marine fuels complicated investment decisions, while ammonia bunkering would require additional storage infrastructure. “I don’t think we will see a mature ammonia market in the next five to 10 years,” he said. “But beyond that, of course, there will be more and more demand for ammonia.” Source: Platts 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: German B100 bunkering surges as marine fuel loophole stays open
articles.summary: ENGINE recorded 169 B100 fuel quality samples in German ports between January and August, up from 16 in the same period last year. articles.body: German B100 bunkering surges as marine fuel loophole stays open in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 ENGINE recorded 169 B100 fuel quality samples in German ports between January and August, up from 16 in the same period last year. B100’s share of German biofuel samples rose from 25% to 73% over this period. ENGINE’s sample data covers only part of Germany’s bunker market. Germany does not release official B100 bunkering figures for the country’s ports. The number of B100 samples in ENGINE’s data can therefore act as an indicator of how demand for the fuel is trending. ENGINE’s samples show five suppliers selling B100 in German ports in January-August, up from three in the same period last year. The rise comes amid what biofuels research firm Prima Markets calls accelerating use of a marine fuel blending loophole in Germany’s greenhouse gas (GHG) quota rules. How does the loophole work? Germany’s GHG quota, which implements the EU’s Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) for transport fuels, requires fuel suppliers to cut their fuel emissions by 12% this year, rising to 17.5% next year. Companies can meet the quota by blending biofuel into diesel and petrol, or by buying credits, known as tickets, from companies that have earned them. Because companies need tickets to meet their quotas, the tickets have a market value. Unlike in the Netherlands, where bunker suppliers can earn tickets by selling biofuels to ships, Germany’s quota levels have been set specifically for land-based transport. Fuel delivered to ships, which is normally tax-exempt, is meant to be outside the quota obligation. But the quota counts fuel based on how it is taxed, not where it is used. Some suppliers instead declare biofuel meant for ships as road fuel and pay road fuel tax on it. This earns them tickets, which they can sell. A ship’s operator pays a price that includes the tax, then claims the tax back from customs once the ship has burned the fuel. “The economics of importing B100 and bio-LNG for use in shipping, but declaring these fuels for road use, voluntarily paying road taxes, and subsequently claiming a tax refund when the fuel is used in shipping, are highly attractive,” Prima Markets analyst Ulrich Arnheiter said. The tickets, called THG certificates, are not cancelled after the fuel is shown to have been used in the maritime sector rather than the road transport sector. Selling these tickets brings in extra revenue for the suppliers. This mechanism has been the primary reason behind the surge in B100 demand in German ports, a market source told ENGINE. The source said a few suppliers have been using this mechanism to supply B100 at cheap prices, while other suppliers see it as a grey area to operate in. The source estimates the mechanism cuts B100 prices by roughly $600-700/mt. Pressure to close the loophole Prima thinks the loophole is one of the reasons THG certificate prices have fallen sharply since early October. It assessed German 2026 Advanced THG certificates at €365/mtCO2e ($399/mtCO2e) on Friday, down 29% from €512/mtCO2e ($560/mtCO2e) on 1 October. Initiative Klimabetrug Stoppen (Stop Climate Fraud Initiative), a German renewables industry group, said on 5 November that the extra certificates are entering an already oversupplied market, distorting it and hurting companies investing in renewable fuels for road transport. It said the government already has the power to exclude fuels used outside land transport and called for a rule from 1 January 2027 based on whether fuel was “demonstrably used in road transport”, backed by checks between customs and the biofuel quota office. “The government can change this without the Bundestag having to act again. It should do so now,” said Marc Schubert, the group’s deputy chair. The group said the practice is not ruled out under current law, and that its demands are aimed at the government rather than individual companies. ENGINE has asked Germany’s environment ministry (BMUKN), which is responsible for the GHG quota, whether it plans to stop fuels used by ships from counting towards the quota and when any change could take effect. The ministry had not responded at the time of writing. The market source ENGINE spoke to expects the loophole to be closed by 2027 and said the extra B100 demand may fall as prices rise again. Source: By Nachiket Tekawade, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: A barrage of transportation disruptions has affected the global economy in recent years. articles.body: Transportation bottlenecks and aggregate shocks in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 A barrage of transportation disruptions has affected the global economy in recent years. This column examines how transportation bottlenecks interact with aggregate shocks, comparing the Commodity Supercycle of the 2000s and the post-pandemic Great Supply Chain Disruption. The spike in freight rates for dry bulk shipping in the former episode was due to scarce shipping capacity, while the latter stemmed from scarce port capacity. Shipping prices rise dramatically when transportation capacity is scarce, while port prices remain much more stable. The constraint matters: when ships are scarce, shipowners have strong incentives to order new vessels, but addressing port scarcity may require government intervention. A barrage of transportation disruptions has affected the global economy in recent years, from the Great Supply Chain Disruption following the COVID-19 pandemic to disruptions in the Red Sea, environmental shocks in critical waterways, and recent tensions around the Strait of Hormuz. The transportation sector, which seemed to carry international trade seamlessly during much of the era of globalisation, has repeatedly emerged as a critical bottleneck. This has happened against a backdrop of large increases in prices and recurring shortages, raising a natural question: how much do transportation disruptions matter in the aggregate, and when do they matter? Maritime transportation is a natural place to look. Ships carry more than 80% of world trade in goods, and transportation accounts for a substantial part of the time required to move inputs across countries. Alessandria et al. (2023), for instance, show that increases in shipping delays raise prices, cause stockouts, and reduce economic activity. Bai et al. (2024) and Ostry et al. (2022) find that increases in shipping costs pass through to inflation. Dunn and Leibovici (2025) have highlighted how disruptions in the Red Sea can reduce effective shipping capacity, and Baslandze and Fuchs (2026) have shown delivery shortfalls can propagate into consumer prices through firms’ pricing decisions. In recent work (Brancaccio et al. 2026), we study how transportation bottlenecks interact with aggregate shocks. A disruption that has limited aggregate effects when the transportation system has spare capacity can propagate widely through the economy when ships or ports are already operating close to their limits. A transportation sector with limited capacity to adjust Our analysis focuses on dry bulk shipping, which transports raw materials such as coal, grain, and iron ore. Dry bulk shipping accounts for roughly one-third of global seaborne trade by volume, and dry bulk carriers account for about 43% of the world fleet’s carrying capacity. Two components determine the sector’s capacity: port infrastructure and the shipping fleet. We provide evidence that both are rigid in the short run. Port capacity expands only slowly. When demand rises, ports cannot quickly add berths, cranes, or storage space. In the data, this rigidity shows up in a simple way: when demand at a port increases, the number of ships being serviced simultaneously changes relatively little, while the queue outside the port grows sharply. The fleet is similarly difficult to expand. Shipbuilding takes several years, and ships are already used intensively. Existing vessels are active more than 90% of the time on average, leaving little reserve capacity that can be activated when demand rises. Shipping markets display a striking pattern: freight rates are stable for long stretches and then spike. Rigidities in transportation offer a natural explanation. When the system has slack, extra demand is absorbed by putting idle capacity to work. When it does not, extra demand creates a shortage, and because capacity cannot expand quickly, rates adjust sharply. Dry bulk shipping saw two pronounced episodes over the past two decades – the 2000s Commodity Supercycle and the Great Supply Chain Disruption after COVID-19 – in which rates rose several-fold before eventually falling back. Then, the question is whether these episodes reflected genuinely scarce transportation capacity, and if so, where the bottleneck was. Measuring transportation capacity To answer this, we model maritime transportation as a queueing network. A shipment must first find a ship. It then has to enter a port, where it may wait before being loaded, and finally the vessel must travel to its destination. Each stage can limit how much trade the transportation system can handle. The framework therefore produces two potential bottlenecks. One comes from ports, where capacity depends on port infrastructure and service times. The other comes from ships, where capacity depends on the size of the fleet but also on how long ships remain occupied travelling or waiting at ports. The capacity of the transportation system is determined by whichever of these two constraints is tighter. This delivers a simple measure of capacity based on observable objects: port infrastructure, port service times, the number of ships, and travel distances. Because these variables are widely available, the measure can be constructed over time and used to gauge how much slack exists in the transportation sector. This framework also helps explain the behaviour of shipping prices. When transportation capacity is slack, freight rates equal the marginal cost of shipping. Moreover, changes in port capacity or fleet size have little effect on prices or trade. Once transportation capacity binds, however, the quantity that can be transported is capped. Freight rates then rise to clear the market, generating the observed spikes. That distinction turns out to be important for understanding both the Great Supply Chain Disruption and the 2000s Commodity Supercycle. The Great Supply Chain Disruption: Ports became the bottleneck As shown in Figure 1, between 2013 and 2020, the transportation system generally had spare capacity. Starting in 2021, this changed. COVID-related labour restrictions and other disruptions increased port service times. At the same time, demand for raw materials rose sharply. Effective port capacity declined, and by 2021, the port constraint became binding for several quarters. The effect on commodity markets was sizeable. In a counterfactual in which transportation capacity is sufficiently high that the constraint does not bind, commodity price inflation between 2019 and 2021–23 is about three percentage points lower, accounting for roughly 13% of the observed increase. But the story is more complicated than it seems. On top of the higher demand and the port disruptions, a contraction in commodity supply due to lockdowns, mine closures, and later the war in Ukraine also affected commodity prices. This interaction matters. The contraction in commodity supply reduced the amount that needed to be transported and therefore partly alleviated pressure on the transportation sector. In a counterfactual without the negative supply shock, commodity prices remain almost as high because the additional production cannot be moved through the already-constrained system. Only when both the supply shock and the transportation constraint are removed does the price increase fall substantially – by 72% – while trade rises by almost 50%. The implication is that transportation capacity can shape the transmission of other aggregate shocks. When transportation is the binding constraint, expanding commodity supply alone may do relatively little to lower prices because the additional output cannot reach consumers. The Commodity Supercycle: Ships were scarce The Commodity Supercycle of the 2000s provides a useful contrast. China’s rapid industrialisation and urbanisation generated a major increase in demand for raw materials such as iron ore and coal. Trade expanded sharply, but this time, the relevant bottleneck was not port infrastructure. It was the fleet. Shipbuilding takes years, so the number of vessels could not adjust quickly enough to the increase in demand. The ship constraint became binding and freight rates rose dramatically. Counterfactual simulations suggest that insufficient transportation capacity accounted for as much as 23% of the increase in commodity prices between 2007 and mid-2008. High freight rates induced a large wave of ship orders (Kalouptsidi 2014). But because of long construction lags, much of this new capacity arrived only after the boom had ended. The dry bulk fleet subsequently expanded dramatically, and the ship constraint did not bind again in the later part of the sample. The comparison between the two episodes is therefore informative. During the Commodity Supercycle, the scarce factor was ships. During the Great Supply Chain Disruption, it was ports. Both generated high freight rates and higher commodity prices, but the source of the bottleneck – and therefore the relevant policy response – was different. Transportation resilience and investment The broader lesson is that transportation infrastructure can have aggregate consequences. What matters is not simply whether the sector experiences a disruption, but whether that disruption pushes the system against its capacity. This also changes how resilience should be measured. A transportation system with substantial slack may absorb a large disruption with relatively modest aggregate effects. A much smaller disruption can be consequential when capacity is already exhausted. The distinction between ships and ports also matters for investment incentives. A striking feature of the data is that shipping prices rise dramatically when transportation capacity is scarce, while port prices remain much more stable – even when ports themselves are the bottleneck. This means that congestion rents are captured differently across the two parts of the system. When ships are scarce, shipowners benefit directly from higher freight rates and have strong incentives to order new vessels. When ports are scarce, the port itself may capture relatively little of the resulting scarcity rent, particularly given the semi-public ownership structure of many ports. As a result, there may be strong private incentives to invest in ships but weaker incentives to expand port infrastructure. This creates potentially important policy implications for port investment (Brancaccio et al. 2025) and port pricing, as explored in Brancaccio et al. (n.d.).1 Transportation bottlenecks are therefore more than local logistics problems. They are a channel through which demand, supply, geopolitical, and infrastructure shocks can affect aggregate prices and trade. The relevant question for policymakers is not simply whether transportation has been disrupted. It is whether the system still has slack – and, when it does not, where the binding constraint lies. articles.body: Banks and public lenders keep billions flowing to fossil-fuel-only ships, new report finds in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 New Solutions for Our Climate research finds that leading commercial banks lent $24 billion to the world’s top container lines, while nearly all of South Korea’s $58 billion in public shipbuilding finance went to fossil-fuel-only vessels. November 23, 2026 (SEOUL) – Private and public financial institutions continue to channel billions of dollars into the construction of ships that can only run on fossil fuels, risking decades of additional emissions from an industry committed to reaching net zero by around 2050. A new report by Solutions for Our Climate (SFOC) examines how financing decisions are shaping the global shipping fleet, finding that climate considerations remain largely absent. Global ship finance totaled approximately $680 billion as of December 2025. The report, Capital at the Helm: Financing Decisions and the Future of Shipping, traces how commercial banks and public financial institutions influence which ships are built and what fuels they run on. Ships ordered today could remain in operation well into the 2040s and 2050s, meaning financing decisions made now will shape the fleet and its emissions for decades. Although the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF) is still pending adoption, its GHG Strategy commits international shipping to reaching net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by or around 2050. Yet an overwhelming majority of new ships are still being built with engines that can only run on fossil fuels. Vessels capable of running on zero- and near-zero-emission (ZNZ) fuels accounted for only around 5% of newbuild orders of 5,000 gross tons or above between 2023 and August 2026. Commercial banks continue lending billions to build fossil-fuel-only ships SFOC examined lending by the ten largest commercial bank creditors to shipping-related entities of the world’s top ten containership groups, including MSC, Maersk, CMA CGM, and Hapag-Lloyd. Between 2016 and 2025, these banks provided $24 billion in loans to those entities. Approximately $12.9 billion across 140 deals was identified as likely related to vessel orders, based on the stated use of proceeds. The groups ordered 737 new vessels between January 2020 and July 2026. Of these, 636 (86%) were only capable of fossil-fuel propulsion. With ships typically operating for 20 to 30 years, these orders risk extending fossil fuel dependence well into the middle of the century. Eight of the ten largest creditors are headquartered in Europe: BNP Paribas, Santander, Société Générale, UniCredit, HSBC, ING, Crédit Agricole, and Standard Chartered. South Korean public finance overwhelmingly supports fossil-fuel-only ships The picture is similar for public finance. South Korea, alongside China and Japan, account for around 90% of global shipbuilding. Between 2015 and 2026, South Korean export credit agencies (ECAs), KEXIM and K-SURE, along with three other public financial institutions, together provided approximately $58 billion in loans and guarantees for newbuilds constructed in Korean shipyards. Of this, $53.8 billion (93%) supported fossil-fuel-only-propelled vessels. In 2025, public financing provided $660 million for ZNZ-capable vessels and $5.3 billion to fossil-fuel-only vessels. Figure: Year-over-year trends of South Korean public financing toward vessel newbuild The country’s shipbuilding output reflects this pattern. Of the 1,593 newbuilds constructed in Korean shipyards over the period, 1,515 (95%) were equipped with engines capable of running only on fossil fuels. But South Korea has already demonstrated its ability to compete in the construction of cleaner ships. According to Clarksons World Fleet Register, Korean shipyards built 26 of the 59 vessels capable of running on ammonia or methanol delivered globally in 2025, ranking second worldwide behind China. The report highlights that South Korea must prioritize public financing support for building ZNZ-capable vessels to maintain its industrial advantage and market competitiveness. Existing financing governance falls short of climate goals A growing number of frameworks, including the EU’s Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR), ask financial institutions to assess climate-related risks in their portfolios. However, as the report finds, many primarily focus on emissions measurement and disclosure rather than preemptive restrictions. They also often overlook a ship’s cumulative emissions over its full operational lifetime. Furthermore, transaction-level information is often opaque for many private financing arrangements. For public finance, the gap is wider still. OECD rules governing ship export credits do not consider a vessel’s fuel type or emissions intensity. The export credit agencies of China, South Korea, and Japan have also not joined voluntary initiatives such as the Net-Zero Export Credit Agencies Alliance. The report points to a precedent for stronger action: in 2021, OECD Participants agreed to end export credit support for unabated coal-fired power plants. SFOC argues that similar restrictions should be considered for new fossil-fuel-only vessels. Valerie Xu, Shipping Policy Researcher at SFOC, said, “Financiers must move beyond retrospective disclosure of their portfolio’s climate impact and take responsibility for what they finance. Both private and public financial institutions must strengthen due diligence criteria for ship financing, with the goal of restricting financial support for vessel newbuilds that can only run on fossil fuels.” SFOC recommends that financial institutions: require robust climate due diligence for newbuild lending; set clear financing restrictions for fossil-fuel-only-propelled vessels; improve transparency through disclosure of their financing policies and transaction-level information; and redirect financing towards green and low-carbon shipping. Source: Solutions for Our Climate (SFOC) 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: UK-EU reset must deliver greater clarity on costs to trade
articles.summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping has responded to the outcome of the UK-EU reset talks, welcoming progress in some areas but calling for greater clarity on the implications for the cost and competitiveness of UK trade. A UK Chamber of Shipping spokesperson said: • The UK-EU reset should ultimately be judged on whether it...
articles.body: UK-EU reset must deliver greater clarity on costs to trade in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 The UK Chamber of Shipping has responded to the outcome of the UK-EU reset talks, welcoming progress in some areas but calling for greater clarity on the implications for the cost and competitiveness of UK trade. A UK Chamber of Shipping spokesperson said: • The UK-EU reset should ultimately be judged on whether it lowers barriers and strengthens the competitiveness of UK trade. For shipping, the outcome is mixed, with some important steps forward but significant cost implications and unanswered questions elsewhere. • Progress towards an SPS agreement should help reduce friction at the border, while recognition of the circumstances facing island routes is welcome, including for lifeline ferry services such as those serving the Isle of Wight. • But businesses will rightly look at the agreement as a whole. We argued ahead of the talks that closer alignment with the EU should reduce unnecessary cost and complexity and make trade easier and more competitive, not simply add costs elsewhere. On Emissions Trading; • The emissions trading measures will have significant implications for shipping and the supply chains on which businesses and consumers depend. Shipping is committed to decarbonisation, but the transition needs to be practical, affordable and internationally aligned, with regulation that supports investment while safeguarding competitiveness. • Linking the UK and EU emissions trading schemes must also address the important differences that remain between them. The UK cannot simply align the costs of the two schemes without looking at the support available to help businesses invest and decarbonise. • We welcome plans for a ‘one-stop shop’ to simplify compliance, but UK shipping must also benefit from comparable support for the transition and greater alignment on allowances, including through the EU’s proposed Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion allowances. Revenues raised from shipping should also be reinvested in the fuels and technologies needed to decarbonise the sector. On the next steps: • We now need much greater detail from Government on how these measures will work in practice, alongside a full assessment of their economic impact. • As the arrangements are developed, protecting essential connectivity and the competitiveness of UK shipping and trade must remain central. Source: UK Chamber of Shipping 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: After COP31 Failure, World Gets Second Chance at Historic Shipping Climate Deal
articles.summary: Two days after COP31 ended without an overarching climate agreement, international experts and advocates called on governments to seize a new opportunity for global climate action: adopting a landmark agreement to cut emissions from international shipping. During a virtual media briefing Tuesday, speakers outlined...
articles.body: After COP31 Failure, World Gets Second Chance at Historic Shipping Climate Deal in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 Two days after COP31 ended without an overarching climate agreement, international experts and advocates called on governments to seize a new opportunity for global climate action: adopting a landmark agreement to cut emissions from international shipping. During a virtual media briefing Tuesday, speakers outlined the prospects for adopting the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, which countries approved in draft form in April 2025 but postponed formally adopting last October following threats from the Trump administration. Unlike the UN climate negotiations, where a lack of consensus derailed an agreement at COP31, the IMO does not require unanimity. If countries cannot reach consensus, the framework can be adopted by a two-thirds majority of eligible parties present and voting. With negotiations underway and a potential adoption decision scheduled for December 4, advocates argued that countries have a realistic path to delivering the climate agreement that eluded negotiators in Turkey. Em Fenton, Senior Director of Climate Diplomacy at Opportunity Green, said: “The Net-Zero Framework is a hard-fought multilateral compromise and – if adopted – could accelerate the global transition to the truly sustainable fuels and technologies of the future whilst delivering justice and equity for all. International negotiations on climate change are complex, fraught, infuriating and essential. A positive outcome at the IMO can protect the very fabric of multilateralism, deliver on states’ legal obligations with respect to climate and reinforce their legal duty to cooperate in the global best interest. We look to them to learn the lessons of COP31 and adopt the Framework without further delay.” “COP31 showed what happens when a few countries use a consensus based process to stand in the way of global progress. But the Net-Zero Framework will come down to a one country, one vote democratic vote,” said Andrew Nazdin of the Glasgow Actions Team. “It’s been negotiated, approved in draft, defended under heavy pressure, and still enjoys majority support from countries around the world. The question now becomes will world leaders stand up to Trump and the petrostates to get this thing approved, including protecting the vulnerable countries they’ll try to bully into voting against it.” Speakers also highlighted the dramatically changed political landscape since October 2025, when the Trump administration threatened countries supporting the framework with tariffs, sanctions, and visa restrictions. Following Trump’s midterm defeat and a Supreme Court ruling limiting his ability to impose tariffs under emergency economic powers legislation, the administration faces diminished leverage and the prospect of increased congressional scrutiny. Meanwhile, the economic case for action is growing stronger. New research from Zero Carbon Analytics estimates that international shipping emissions between 1990 and 2020 have caused $963 billion in global economic damages. The analysis warns that continued emissions could ultimately impose costs greater than those of implementing the framework, particularly as climate impacts intensify. “We need to be clear that there is a cost of inaction, and that the evidence stacks up against that pathway,” said Tom Grylls, Opportunity Green Director of Analytics. Sebastian Grajales of Climate Reality pointed to a new report finding that clean shipping and port electrification can support over 110,000 new jobs in the United States, as well as a new executive order aimed at strengthening domestic shipbuilding and maritime workforce. “Shipping is about to become one of the biggest clean energy markets on Earth,” Grajales said. “But investment needs certainty. The IMO Net-Zero Framework would provide that certainty. Once adopted, it would set a clear global fuel standard, reward zero- and near-zero-emission fuels and raise an estimated $11 billion to $12 billion a year in its early years for clean-fuel production, port upgrades, seafarer training, and support for developing countries.” Even the shipping industry is calling for global action. On November 18, nine major international maritime trade associations, including the International Chamber of Shipping, BIMCO, and the World Shipping Council, issued a joint statement urging governments to establish stable, enforceable global regulations to support shipping decarbonization and provide certainty for investment. Speakers stressed that the stakes extend far beyond the shipping industry, particularly for developing countries already confronting the impacts of climate change. Dola Oluteye, Senior Fellow at University College London’s Energy Institute, said: “For Africa, climate inaction is existential. COP31 failed to produce an agreed text, and the IMO talks must not repeat that failure. The continent is home to most of the world’s least developed countries and depends heavily on shipping for its trade, yet owns little of the fleet. Surrounded with vast natural resources that can transform the continents fortunes with a global policy that can catalyse industrial growth. This shipping decarbonisation policy offers Africa a reset: the chance, given her abundant resources, to industrialise along a green pathway. That promise holds only if the transition is just and equitable, and if African states help to design its architecture instead of taking instructions from others. Africa must exercise her sovereign right to choose her own future, and the future worth choosing is green.” Soujanya Chitumadugula, sustainability practitioner and community leader, shared about her personal experience of a climate event which stayed with her and shaped her views in understanding and participating in climate action. In October 2014, Cyclone Hudhud hit Visakhapatnam. In a few hours, much of the city’s tree cover was lost, buildings were badly damaged, and it took years to build back. Along other coastlines, families woke up to a new shoreline. “Hudhud wasn’t caused by shipping,” Chitumadugula said. “But it showed what the new reality looks like, and who feels it first… We don’t have to wait for another disaster to take action. My ask to governments is simple: adopt strong rules, make major polluters pay, and put frontline communities at the table when the money is allocated. Now is the time to follow through.” What happens next Through November 27: Technical negotiations at the IMO in London. November 30, 8:00 AM: Activists greet IMO delegates with massive banners and calls to action with compelling imagery and messaging. Every person walking into negotiations will be confronted by unmissable banners calling on delegates to pass the net-zero framework now on the sea wall and Lambeth bridge. They will also see massive signs and rubber ducks urging delegates to ignore efforts by the lame-duck President Trump to delay or kill the framework. November 30–December 3: The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee meets, accompanied by planned demonstrations urging countries to adopt the framework. December 4: A special session to consider formal adoption is provisionally scheduled, with a further mobilization planned outside the IMO. Source: Glasgow Actions Team 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

If countries cannot reach consensus, the framework can be adopted by a two-thirds majority of eligible parties present and voting.

With negotiations underway and a potential adoption decision scheduled for December 4, advocates argued that countries have a realistic path to delivering the climate agreement that eluded negotiators in Turkey.

articles.title: Toxic port pollution costs Europe €2.5bn a year in health and environmental damages – study
articles.summary: Commercial ships docked in European ports inflict €2.5 billion a year in societal and environmental costs, according to new research by T&E. While upcoming EU port rules will cut at-berth damages by 40% by 2030, most vessels remain exempt. Previous research has shown that residents living close to a commercial...
articles.body: Toxic port pollution costs Europe €2.5bn a year in health and environmental damages – study in Port News 25/11/2026 Commercial ships docked in European ports inflict €2.5 billion a year in societal and environmental costs, according to new research by T&E. While upcoming EU port rules will cut at-berth damages by 40% by 2030, most vessels remain exempt. Previous research has shown that residents living close to a commercial harbour already face significantly higher risks of cardiovascular and respiratory mortality [1]. Tightening port pollution rules would save society billions and protect the health of port communities, says T&E. Instead of plugging into the electrical grid when they dock, thousands of commercial vessels run diesel generators around the clock to power onboard systems. These idling engines release harmful pollution directly into neighbouring coastal and port communities. Analysis of Europe’s 100 largest ports shows that Rotterdam is the most polluted with costs at €350 million, followed by Antwerp (€220 million), Marseille (€120 million), Hamburg (€120 million), and Genoa (€110 million). According to the report, removing loopholes in the EU rules would save Europe €1.56bn in health and climate costs. Under current EU rules, outlined in the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), only large container ships, ferries and cruise ships are required to plug into dockside electricity sockets, meaning oil and gas tankers, bulk carriers, car carriers and other cargo ships are left out entirely. Requirements to connect should be progressively extended to all ship types in the upcoming review to cut emissions and grant ports the necessary long-term predictability. Eloi Nordé, shipping policy officer at T&E, said: “Port communities are paying the price for ships running their engines 24/7 at port. Fossil fuels only seem cheap because companies offload health and climate costs onto the public. Fortunately, the solution already exists. Plugging ships into shoreside electric power would save society billions and make port cities far healthier to live in.” On paper, marine fuels appear less costly than drawing electricity from the port grid. However, this is largely because the associated healthcare and environmental burdens are absorbed by the local population rather than ship operators. Once these external costs are factored into energy pricing, generating power from fossil fuels at dock is twice as costly as using shore electricity. This policy gap creates a lot of planning uncertainty for EU port authorities and electricity grid operators. Without a predictable policy progressively including all vessel types, ports are disincentivised from making long-term investments in green infrastructure, says T&E. The EU will review the regulation at the end of this year. T&E urges EU policymakers to use the AFIR review to expand shore power to all ships, batteries, and boilers, backed by national port electrification roadmaps before 2032. Its call is echoed today in a joint letter to the European Commission from the Clean Port Cities (CPC) coalition, uniting industry, civil society, and maritime and energy stakeholders including DFDS and Green Transition Denmark, urging predictable shore power timelines for all vessels, battery charging rules, and faster grid access. articles.summary: The Port of Gothenburg is investing in overhead line infrastructure for the container terminal’s handling tracks in a move that will boost capacity, cut emissions and improve the efficiency of rail operations. The investment will enable electric locomotives to run directly to and from the terminal, removing the need...
articles.body: Port of Gothenburg invests in electrified rail access to the container terminal in Port News 25/11/2026 The Port of Gothenburg is investing in overhead line infrastructure for the container terminal’s handling tracks in a move that will boost capacity, cut emissions and improve the efficiency of rail operations. The investment will enable electric locomotives to run directly to and from the terminal, removing the need for diesel locomotives or detours via the port departure yard. The project is designed to create more efficient rail flows within the port area and support continued growth in rail freight volumes. By extending the overhead line infrastructure to the container terminal’s handling tracks, electric locomotives will be able to operate all the way to and from the terminal. This will reduce the need for shunting via the port departure yard, freeing up capacity, shortening turnaround times and lowering carbon emissions. The container terminal is operated by APM Terminals and handles around 80 trains per week, linking the port with more than 20 destinations across Sweden. “It is very positive that the final stretch into the terminal is now being electrified. When electric locomotives can run all the way to our fossil-free container handling operation, another fossil fuel dependency is removed from the transport flow. This gives our customers better opportunities to reduce emissions from their transports and strengthens rail as a sustainable and competitive alternative,” says Birna Ödefors, Managing Director of APM Terminals Gothenburg. Here, containers are transferred between rail and sea at the container terminal. Soon, the conditions for this will be even better. Photo: The Port of Gothenburg. Rail freight volumes continue to grow Last year, a record 529,000 TEU were transported to and from the port by rail, and volumes have continued to increase in 2026. As demand grows, so too does the need to make better use of existing infrastructure. “This will be an important step in strengthening the competitiveness of rail in the port. Through more efficient traffic arrangements, we can create better conditions for both growth and sustainable transport,” says Robert Sommar, Railway Manager at the Port of Gothenburg. The investment is expected to cut total turnaround times for container rail shuttles by up to 30 minutes, while also enabling longer trains to be handled. Today, train length is limited by the 630-metre tracks in the departure yard. The new solution will improve conditions for handling trains of up to 750 metres. The time savings will come from allowing trains to depart directly from the container terminal, reducing time spent in the departure yard. The project includes the installation of around 1,250 metres of overhead line infrastructure, along with 38 line masts and associated foundations. It also includes upgrades to level crossing protection systems and a new emergency access road, further enhancing safety and resilience for both road and rail traffic in the area. The British newspaper Financial Times (FT) reported on the 22nd that hacking attacks targeting U.S. ports, oil tankers and major shipping companies have surged in recent months, exposing vulnerabilities in the aging networks that support international trade. The Port of Corpus Christi in Texas, the largest U.S. crude oil export port, which ships 2.3 million barrels of crude a day, faces hundreds to thousands of attempted system intrusions daily. Hackers are trying to penetrate its networks or trick employees into handing over system access. The tactics range from automated attacks that randomly enter passwords or overload computer networks to sophisticated intrusions aimed at stealing or deleting data. Port of Corpus Christi CEO Kent Britton said, “Hackers are probing the system here and there, looking for vulnerabilities. It will get more complicated when artificial intelligence (AI) comes into play.” Experts have pointed to Iran, North Korea and China, among others, as being behind the hacking attacks. Cybersecurity firm Shieldworks said the Russian hacking group “NoName057(16)” threatened European shipping companies in October. The FT noted that a recent series of major technical disruptions in the U.S. has laid bare the vulnerabilities of the country’s critical digital infrastructure. An earlier U.S. air traffic control system outage stranded hundreds of thousands of people, while Microsoft (MS) Outlook was down for nearly 24 hours. The banking system of JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank, also suffered major disruption due to a software error. Although the incidents have not been confirmed to be directly linked to cyberattacks, concern is growing because hackers are using AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than companies can respond. Maritime cybersecurity incidents rose 17% last year from the previous year, according to the U.S. Coast Guard. In August, the U.S. Coast Guard also investigated a cyberattack on two tankers carrying crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) from the Mediterranean to Galveston, Texas, near the Strait of Gibraltar. articles.body: PSA Vietnam and Lach Huyen International Logistics & Industrial Park (LHF) have broken ground on a new container terminal in Hai Phong, northern Vietnam. The terminal, known as Haiphong Xuan Cau PSA International Container Terminal (HXPICT), will have an annual handling capacity of 4.7 million TEUs. Construction officially began with a groundbreaking ceremony on 23 November 2026. The first two berths are expected to begin operations in 2028. The project will improve connections between northern Vietnam’s industrial areas and international shipping routes. New terminal to support Vietnam’s growing trade The development follows an agreement announced in July 2026 between PSA and LHF to jointly develop and operate four deep-sea container berths at Lach Huyen Port, as previously reported by Container News . The project brings together PSA’s international port network and LHF’s industrial and logistics facilities. The partners aim to connect the terminal with nearby industrial areas, creating a more integrated transport and logistics network. “The development of HXPICT is an important milestone in advancing PSA’s Node to Network strategy, which seeks to connect ports and supply chain hubs into an integrated global network,” said Nelson Quek, Regional CEO, Southeast Asia, PSA International. Quek said the project would strengthen PSA’s presence in northern Vietnam and improve connections with global markets. Nguyen Vinh Hau, General Director of LHF, confirmed that the partners aim to bring the first two berths into operation in 2028. He also highlighted plans to connect the deepwater terminal with the nearby non-tariff zone and industrial park. Once developed, HXPICT will provide additional container handling capacity in northern Vietnam and support the region’s growing logistics needs.

articles.body: NextGeo Gets $12.7M Offshore Survey Job for Spain-France Hydrogen Link Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 25, 2026 Italian offshore services provider Next Geosolutions (NextGeo) has secured a contract worth approximately $12.7 million (€11.6 million) from BarMar for offshore survey work supporting the development of a planned hydrogen pipeline connecting Spain and France. The contract covers an integrated survey campaign along an approximately 366-kilometre offshore corridor between Barcelona, Spain, and Fos-sur-Mer, France. The scope includes geophysical, geotechnical and UXO surveys, grab sampling, remotely operated vehicle (ROV) inspections and surveys of crossings with existing subsea infrastructure. The data collected will be used to characterise seabed and sub-seabed conditions to support the planning and design of the future pipeline. NextGeo will deploy two dedicated vessels for the offshore operations, which are expected to begin by the end of 2026. The campaign is currently scheduled for completion between the end of the second quarter and the beginning of the third quarter of 2027, depending on any additional work requested during execution. The BarMar pipeline forms part of H2med, a cross-border initiative designed to connect hydrogen networks in the Iberian Peninsula with northwestern Europe. The project is being developed by BarMar S.A.S., whose shareholders are NaTran, Enagás and Teréga. H2med is included on the European Union's list of Projects of Common Interest, with BarMar providing the planned maritime hydrogen transport connection between Spain and France. The award marks NextGeo's first contract with BarMar, expanding its offshore survey activities into hydrogen infrastructure development.

articles.body: A container’s journey does not end when a vessel reaches port. After discharge, it must move through a terminal, reach an inland destination by road, rail or barge, and eventually return to a depot or find another export load. Each transfer creates costs and operational dependencies. For shipping lines and cargo owners, the economics of this journey increasingly depend on how efficiently the different assets and operators work together. Dedicated logistics networks offer one way to coordinate these movements. They connect container terminals, inland depots, transport capacity, empty-container facilities and digital systems through company-owned assets, long-term partnerships or reserved third-party capacity. The objective is to improve control over container flows while making transport and infrastructure resources more productive. Utilisation Is Where the Economics Begin The scale of container movement makes coordination increasingly important. UN Trade and Development estimates that ports worldwide handled approximately 920 million TEUs in 2024, representing a 6.9% increase over 2023. Moving this volume through maritime gateways and inland corridors requires dependable connections between terminals, depots and transport providers. One persistent cost is the movement of empty containers. A 2026 study published in Transportation Journal, analysing container truck movements in Sweden between 2016 and 2019, found that empty containers accounted for 44–46% of vehicle journeys and approximately 30–35% of vehicle kilometres. These figures are specific to the Swedish market and study period, rather than a global estimate. They nevertheless demonstrate how much road capacity can be consumed without moving loaded cargo. Dedicated networks can help address this inefficiency by coordinating container availability, depot locations, return movements and inland transport schedules. An import container discharged at a port, for example, may be repositioned for an export customer rather than moved empty to another location. Rail and barge services can also support larger consolidated flows where volumes and infrastructure permit. However, dedicated capacity only improves utilisation when cargo volumes are sufficiently dense and predictable. Trade imbalances, seasonal demand and uneven import-export flows can leave trucks, depots, rail capacity and handling equipment underused. Ownership Versus Outsourcing Is a Financial Trade-Off Building an in-house logistics network gives shipping lines or large cargo owners greater control over container yards, drayage, inland terminals and transport schedules. It can support priority access, coordinated equipment positioning and more predictable service commitments. For operators handling stable volumes along concentrated trade corridors, those advantages may justify investment in terminals, fleets, rail capacity and container-handling infrastructure. The risk is fixed-cost exposure. Owned facilities require land, equipment, maintenance, insurance, labour and technology, regardless of whether volumes remain consistently high. When demand declines or trade flows become imbalanced, underutilised assets can quickly weaken the financial return. Outsourcing offers a different cost structure. Shipping lines and cargo owners can access an established provider’s trucks, depots, warehouses and intermodal relationships without financing every asset themselves. Providers serving multiple customers can also combine volumes across routes and improve resource utilisation. The limitation is reduced control over capacity allocation and operating priorities, particularly when transport or terminal resources become scarce. A wider indication of the importance of digital coordination appears in Vyansa Intelligence’s Global Connected Fleet Telematics Market Report . The research identifies transportation and logistics as a key end-user segment, covering applications such as fleet tracking and visibility, vehicle health monitoring, predictive maintenance, and route optimisation and dispatch. Its 2026 market assessment estimates that solutions account for 75% of the connected fleet telematics offering segment. While this figure covers connected fleets across industries rather than container transport specifically, it highlights the growing role of digital systems in coordinating the vehicles and assets supporting port-to-inland movements . A hybrid approach may therefore be more practical. Shipping lines can retain control over strategically important depots or high-volume corridors while contracting variable trucking, rail or barge capacity. The balance depends on cargo density, asset utilisation and the cost of maintaining reliable access. Port-to-Inland Integration Is Taking Different Forms Industry developments show how these arrangements are being built. MEDLOG, part of the MSC Group, operates an inland network spanning more than 90 countries. The company reports transporting over 10 million TEUs annually and maintaining 471 operating sites, including container yards, rail and barge terminals, warehouses and trucking facilities . Its Inland Terminal Paris-Bruyères in France provides a practical example. The 11-hectare facility combines road, rail and barge transportation, with a two-track rail terminal and a 230-metre river quay. It has an annual capacity of more than 100,000 TEUs and connects the Port of Le Havre with inland destinations across Europe. This illustrates how investment in inland infrastructure can extend a maritime network beyond the port boundary. A different model is emerging in Cambodia. On 17 November 2026, CMA CGM Group and Royal Railway signed a memorandum of understanding to assess a rail-connected logistics platform in Phnom Penh. The proposed facility would include a dry port, container-handling yard, empty-container depot, container freight station and rail-connected handling infrastructure. The development is intended to strengthen connections between inland production and consumption centres and the Port of Sihanoukville . The arrangement also illustrates how infrastructure responsibilities can be divided. Royal Railway is expected to provide and maintain rail access and related infrastructure, while CMA CGM Inland Services will lead the operational concept, commercial feasibility assessment and business planning. The project remains at the assessment stage, with no confirmed construction timetable. What Operators Should Measure Before Committing For shipping lines, freight forwarders and cargo owners, the financial assessment should extend beyond the quoted transport rate. Loaded and empty movements, asset utilisation, end-to-end cost per TEU, terminal dwell, container turnaround time and service-level performance all influence the actual return on a dedicated network. Shipping lines should identify high-volume routes where dedicated infrastructure can support consistent utilisation. Freight forwarders can benefit from reserved third-party capacity and shared depot access without assuming ownership of transport assets. Cargo owners should assess whether improved equipment availability and delivery reliability justify longer contractual commitments. The economics of dedicated logistics networks ultimately depend on how effectively port, container and inland transport systems operate as one chain. Ownership can provide control, while outsourcing can provide flexibility and scale. Neither guarantees efficiency. The strongest model is the one that moves more loaded containers through reliable connections while keeping idle capacity, empty repositioning and avoidable handling costs under control. Shammi Thakur is the Research Director at Vyansa Intelligence, with over 15 years of experience in market research, strategic intelligence and industry analysis. His work includes maritime and logistics research, tracking container shipping developments, port operations, intermodal connectivity and the factors shaping global supply chain decisions.
takeaways: A container’s journey does not end when a vessel reaches port.
After discharge, it must move through a terminal, reach an inland destination by road, rail or barge, and eventually return to a depot or find another export load.
Each transfer creates costs and operational dependencies.

articles.title: Interview: NYSHEX sees growing momentum in container freight futures
articles.summary: As volatility continues to reshape container shipping, freight futures and options are attracting growing interest as tools for managing costs and market uncertainty. In the latest episode of CN Talks, Container News welcomed Gordon Downes, Co-Founder and CEO of NYSHEX, and Rich Heath, Vice President of Financial...
articles.body: As volatility continues to reshape container shipping, freight futures and options are attracting growing interest as tools for managing costs and market uncertainty. In the latest episode of CN Talks, Container News welcomed Gordon Downes, Co-Founder and CEO of NYSHEX, and Rich Heath, Vice President of Financial Products, for a discussion on the evolving role of financial instruments in ocean freight. Hosted by Antonia Saratsopoulou, Managing Editor of Container News, and Giannis Nikolakis, CEO of Container News, the roundtable explored freight market volatility, risk management, benchmark reliability and the outlook for 2027. Watch in full screen on YouTube. Growing interest in freight futures According to Downes, the extreme volatility experienced since 2020 has exposed the limitations of traditional freight contracting. As a result, the industry is showing greater interest in index-linked agreements and financial tools designed to manage price fluctuations. Heath highlighted the early development of NYFI-linked futures, noting that more than 10,000 TEUs of futures had been traded since their launch in April 2026. Although the market remains at an early stage, he pointed to growing interest from shippers, freight forwarders and carriers. The discussion also examined how futures and options could help companies manage their freight budgets for 2027. In particular, the guests explained how financial hedging can offer protection against rate increases without changing the underlying physical shipment. Why reliable freight indices matter Another key topic was the importance of trustworthy freight benchmarks. Heath explained how differences between an index and the freight rates actually paid by shippers can affect the effectiveness of a hedge. Meanwhile, Downes discussed the importance of transparency, governance and transaction-based data when indices are used to settle financial contracts. The conversation also explored whether the development of a more liquid futures market could eventually influence how carriers and shippers negotiate physical freight contracts. What lies ahead for container shipping? Looking towards 2027, the participants examined geopolitical uncertainty and the potential impact of changing shipping routes on freight market expectations. The discussion also addressed a possible broader return to the Suez Canal and how carriers might respond to changes in available capacity. Heath explained why the futures curve should be viewed as an indicator of market sentiment rather than a definitive forecast of future freight rates. Finally, the guests considered the challenges facing wider adoption of freight derivatives and what it would take for these instruments to become an established part of the container shipping market. Watch the full CN Talks roundtable with Gordon Downes and Rich Heath to discover how freight futures could reshape risk management, why reliable benchmarks matter and what the industry should be watching as 2027 approaches.

articles.summary: One of shipping’s most vocal proponents of decarbonisation has conceded that its 2050 net zero ambitions are unlikely to be realised, just days ahead of crucial environmental negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). Speaking at the Assises de l’économie de la mer in Montpellier yesterday, CMA...
articles.body: Containers Environment Europe CMA CGM’s Saadé concedes 2050 net zero target is out of reach Sam Chambers November 25, 2026 0 571 1 minute read One of shipping’s most vocal proponents of decarbonisation has conceded that its 2050 net zero ambitions are unlikely to be realised, just days ahead of crucial environmental negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). Speaking at the Assises de l’économie de la mer in Montpellier yesterday, CMA CGM chairman and CEO Rodolphe Saadé put the investment required to decarbonise global shipping at more than $1trn. “We must be realistic: under current circumstances, we will not be able to meet our targets by 2050,” Saadé said. The French shipping magnate cited geopolitical conflicts lengthening voyages and driving up operating costs, the absence of a unified international regulatory framework and the slow development of low-carbon fuels. CMA CGM has already committed nearly $30bn to LNG- and methanol-powered newbuilds, with more than 200 dual-fuel vessels scheduled to be in its fleet by 2030. The Marseille-headquartered carrier operates more than 700 containerships, of which over 400 are owned. The admission comes ahead of next Monday’s opening of the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting in London, where member states will attempt to overcome divisions surrounding the proposed Net-Zero Framework.< Saadé also expressed concern about the future of the French flag, criticising recurring uncertainty surrounding France’s tonnage tax regime. He stressed that containership investments typically involve commitments spanning 25 years, while employing French petty officers adds €2m annually to a ship’s operating costs. According to Saadé, tonnage tax regimes cover 86% of the global fleet and are in place in 22 European countries. In September, CMA CGM dropped plans to register seven large newbuilds under the French flag, citing additional taxation. articles.body: Europe Finance and Insurance Gas British sanctions put $390m of Dynagas charter revenues at risk Sam Chambers November 25, 2026 0 479 1 minute read With little more than five weeks to go before Britain tightens its sanctions on the transportation of Russian LNG, George Procopiou-backed Dynagas LNG Partners is still seeking replacement insurance for two vessels serving the Yamal LNG project. The New York-listed shipowner, in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission yesterday, warned that failure to secure alternative cover could ultimately result in a default under its debt agreements. The two 2013-built, 155,000 cu m LNG carriers, Yenisei River and Lena River, are employed on long-term charters to Yamal Trade through to 2033 and 2034, respectively. Both vessels currently have British protection and indemnity (P&I) and hull and machinery insurance, which will no longer be permitted to cover shipments of Russian-origin LNG from January 1 unless an applicable exemption or licence is available. The two charters accounted for approximately 34% of Dynagas’s revenues in the opening nine months of this year and represent 56% of its $700m contracted revenue backlog The shipowner warned that a failure to secure replacement insurance could result in off-hire claims, litigation or the premature termination of the charters. Complicating matters for the international marine insurance market is the divergence between British and European Union sanctions regimes, with Brussels allowing certain longstanding contracts covering Russian LNG shipments to third countries to continue until at least July next year. Dynagas, meanwhile, has been growing its exposure to American LNG exports, with two of its six vessels now employed on long-term charters with Rio Grande LNG in Texas. articles.title: Geneva Dry: Gestion Maritime’s Danilo Fumarola discusses dry bulk’s rising cost base
articles.summary: Gestion Maritime’s Danilo Fumarola discusses dry bulk’s relatively favourable supply fundamentals, rising breakevens and the opportunities emerging from geopolitical volatility. Dry bulk shipping could offer a greater degree of stability than other shipping sectors over the coming years, but a favourable fleet supply...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Maritime CEO Geneva Dry: Gestion Maritime’s Danilo Fumarola discusses dry bulk’s rising cost base Splash November 25, 2026 0 282 2 minutes read Gestion Maritime’s Danilo Fumarola discusses dry bulk’s relatively favourable supply fundamentals, rising breakevens and the opportunities emerging from geopolitical volatility. Dry bulk shipping could offer a greater degree of stability than other shipping sectors over the coming years, but a favourable fleet supply picture should not obscure the mounting pressures on shipowners’ bottom lines, cautions Danilo Fumarola, CEO of Monaco-based Gestion Maritime Group. Speaking ahead of next April’s Geneva Dry, where he will participate in the coal session, Fumarola points to constrained shipbuilding capacity, an ageing fleet and persistent disruptions to global trade as factors underpinning the sector’s prospects. The substantial number of bulk carriers delivered between 2010 and 2015 is edging closer to the 20-year mark, while securing newbuilding berths is becoming increasingly challenging. Nevertheless, Fumarola harbours concerns about the anomalies developing in the global shipbuilding market, not least the risks associated with China’s dominance. Gestion Maritime itself recently ventured into the ultramax segment, ordering three 64,000 dwt vessels from China’s Nantong Xiangyu Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering for delivery in 2028 and 2029. Geopolitical disruptions, Fumarola says, have the potential to generate considerable freight rate volatility, creating attractive opportunities for buyers and sellers of tonnage, albeit accompanied by heightened risks. Of more immediate concern are rising breakevens. Higher financing and operating costs are putting pressure on profitability, while volatile bunker prices and supply chain inefficiencies, particularly port congestion, are complicating commercial decision-making. The volatility in fuel prices could, however, prove a catalyst for greater investment in energy-saving technologies. Equipment previously dismissed on financial grounds warrants fresh scrutiny, Fumarola says, with the economic case for retrofitting even older tonnage becoming increasingly compelling. The Gestion Maritime boss believes these shifting market dynamics make opportunities for industry participants to exchange views particularly valuable. For Fumarola, the attraction of Geneva Dry extends beyond the formal conference programme. Sharing market intelligence with fellow shipowners, operators and commodity traders helps participants identify emerging trends, while bringing together different players from across the dry bulk value chain can sow the seeds of future commercial cooperation. The fourth edition of Geneva Dry takes place on April 27 and 28, with fuel efficiency, risk management, ship investment and the changing dynamics of global commodity trades featuring prominently on the agenda. articles.body: Containers Europe Maersk storms into megamax league Adis Ajdin November 25, 2026 0 1,391 1 minute read Maersk Maersk Danish liner giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed an order for 12 ultra-large containerships of 24,000 teu, marking its entry into the largest boxship segment with an investment estimated at around $2.9bn. The Copenhagen-based group said the dual-fuel vessels would be delivered in 2030 and 2031, becoming the biggest ships in its fleet. Each vessel will be equipped with engines capable of running on conventional marine fuel or LNG, with the 12-ship series adding 288,000 teu of nominal capacity. Maersk has declined to identify the shipbuilder or disclose the contract value. Shipbuilding sources have previously put the price of the vessels at around $240m apiece. The order follows weeks of negotiations with Chinese shipbuilders, with both Hengli Heavy Industries and Hudong-Zhonghua linked to the project. Earlier market reports pointed to a possible 12-ship contract with options for another dozen, although Maersk’s latest confirmation covers only the initial 12 vessels. The move represents a significant departure from the carrier’s previous preference for slightly smaller ships offering greater deployment flexibility. Its largest existing containerships, the second-generation Triple-E vessels, have capacity of around 20,500 teu. The latest deal adds to Maersk’s renewed appetite for newbuildings after years of comparatively restrained ordering. In September, the company confirmed contracts for 26 LNG dual-fuel ships of 18,600 teu (pictured), scheduled for delivery in 2029 and 2030. That followed an order for eight vessels of the same size at China’s New Times Shipbuilding in February. Including the latest megamax series, Maersk has now confirmed 46 containership newbuildings during 2026, representing a combined nominal capacity of more than 920,000 teu. The orders come against a backdrop of record contracting across the container sector, with the global newbuilding orderbook already exceeding 15m teu and further large-scale investments being pursued by the industry’s biggest carriers. articles.body: Operations Shipping’s glass ceiling proves stubbornly resilient Sam Chambers November 25, 2026 0 301 1 minute read Women are losing ground in key commercial and technical roles at maritime companies despite reporting greater inclusion in the workplace, according to the latest annual review from the Diversity Study Group (DSG). The seventh edition of the Annual DEI in Maritime Review, which surveyed nearly 1,700 shore-based employees across 11 organisations, identifies a seemingly impenetrable glass ceiling at head of department level, where women account for just 14.6% of respondents. Female representation in technical and fleet management positions has fallen from 22.4% last year to 13.2%, while in commercial departments the proportion has dropped from 37.9% to 28.4%. Female representation in IT has almost halved since 2023. More encouragingly, over 90% of female respondents feel encouraged to contribute ideas for the first time, while 93% report having a supportive peer group. Another recurring theme in the annual survey is what DSG describes as the “squeezed middle”, with mid-career employees expressing the greatest frustration over stalled careers, salary discrepancies, favouritism and management behaviour. Employees who have not had a personal development conversation with their manager in the previous six months are considerably less likely to feel their contribution is valued, at 61%, compared with 89% among those who have. Despite the increasingly polarised political debate surrounding diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), DSG concluded that maritime employers are generally making steady progress towards more inclusive workplaces, warning against complacency during uncertain times.
