According to Dynamar ‘s November 2026 edition of DynaLiners Monthly, container freight rates from Ningbo-Zhoushan to the Middle East averaged US$5,243.69 per 40-foot container in October, representing a 453.5% increase compared with the same month in 2025. The figures reveal a market in which geographical exposure is becoming increasingly important, challenging the usefulness of global freight averages as indicators of actual transportation costs. The widening geographical divide The Middle East recorded the largest annual increase among the trade lanes presented in the Ningbo Containerised Freight Index (NCFI) breakdown. Freight rates towards the Red Sea increased by 168.7% year-on-year, while shipments to India and Pakistan recorded an increase of 209.9%. The China Containerised Freight Index (CCFI) reinforces this picture. Its Middle East component increased by 307.1% compared with October 2025, significantly outperforming the overall index’s annual increase of 87%. However, the same degree of upward pressure is not evident across all major trade corridors. The CCFI components for North Europe and the Mediterranean declined between September and October, despite remaining considerably above their respective levels a year earlier. Similarly, Drewry’s World Container Index averaged US$4,457 per 40-foot container in October, slightly below September’s average of US$4,477. More recent developments, highlighted in Container News’ latest freight market assessment , point to continued downward pressure on global benchmarks, particularly across the Transpacific trade. The divergence suggests that the global container market is increasingly characterised by regional pricing cycles rather than a uniform movement in freight rates. The cost of uncertainty Uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, combined with the operational challenges associated with Red Sea navigation, provides important context for understanding the extraordinary increases observed across Middle Eastern trade corridors. Although Dynamar’s figures do not isolate the individual causes of these increases, operational disruption and changes to carrier networks are relevant factors when assessing regional freight pricing. As previously reported by Container News, Maersk introduced emergency freight rates in response to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz , citing additional expenses associated with alternative transportation arrangements, storage, insurance and vessel chartering. For cargo owners, the consequences extend beyond the headline ocean freight rate. Uncertainty surrounding transit times, equipment availability and potential changes to service configurations can complicate procurement and inventory planning. Carrier pricing announcements also illustrate the continuing commercial pressures across the region. According to Dynamar, Maersk announced a Peak Season Surcharge of US$1,000 per TEU on shipments from the Far East to the Middle East, effective November 16. Meanwhile, announced freight adjustments affecting shipments between the Middle East and North America demonstrate how pricing pressures can extend across interconnected trade corridors. These announced increases do not necessarily translate into equivalent increases in realised freight rates, but they provide an indication of carriers’ pricing intentions. An increasingly fragmented market What makes the current environment particularly significant is the coexistence of elevated freight rates, fleet expansion and a strengthening containership charter market. Dynamar recorded the delivery of 21 containerships representing a combined capacity of 169,200 TEU during October. At the same time, both the Harpex and Braemar’s BOX Index reached their highest reported levels of 2026. Additional vessel capacity could help alleviate freight pricing pressures. However, the geographical distribution of that capacity, operational restrictions and the availability of reliable shipping services are equally important. This distinction is particularly relevant to the gradual return of container shipping services to the Suez Canal. As highlighted in a recent market assessment by Sogese , shorter Asia–Europe voyages could release effective vessel capacity and limit the ability of carriers to secure announced freight rate increases. However, an improvement in capacity availability on the Asia–Europe corridor would not necessarily resolve operational challenges affecting Middle Eastern destinations. A growing global fleet does not guarantee lower transportation costs across every trade lane. This distinction could become increasingly important as carriers determine where to deploy additional tonnage and how to balance commercial opportunities against operational risks. What this means for 2027 The October figures should not be interpreted as evidence that Middle Eastern freight rates will continue rising indefinitely. In fact, the average rate from Ningbo to the Middle East declined from US$5,334.85 in September to US$5,243.69 in October. Rates towards the Red Sea, India and Pakistan also registered monthly declines. Nevertheless, their exceptionally elevated year-on-year levels highlight how far regional freight pricing remains from the conditions observed in late 2025. The coexistence of monthly declines and substantial annual increases presents a particularly complex environment for shippers entering their next contract negotiation cycle. A recovery in regional shipping conditions could release capacity and reduce transportation costs. Conversely, renewed disruption could sustain regional freight premiums even if broader global benchmarks continue to decline. Looking ahead to 2027, the central question may not simply be whether global container freight rates rise or fall, but which trade corridors remain exposed to persistent operational uncertainty and which benefit from additional capacity and improving network efficiency. For carriers, freight forwarders and beneficial cargo owners, understanding these geographical differences could become increasingly important when negotiating contracts, allocating capacity and managing transportation risks. The direction of global freight benchmarks may tell only part of the story. Where cargo is moving, how it is transported and which operational risks it encounters could increasingly determine the price of container shipping.

articles.title: EU targets shadow fleet and Russian-insured tankers in new sanctions package
articles.summary: The European Commission has proposed further restrictions on Russia’s maritime and energy sectors as part of its 22nd sanctions package against the country. The proposed measures include adding more than 70 vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet to the European Union’s sanctions list. The Commission is also seeking...
articles.body: The European Commission has proposed further restrictions on Russia’s maritime and energy sectors as part of its 22nd sanctions package against the country. The proposed measures include adding more than 70 vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet to the European Union’s sanctions list. The Commission is also seeking to prohibit all tanker vessels insured in Russia, extending its efforts to restrict the maritime transportation of Russian energy products and limit access to supporting services. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the package would expand the existing energy services ban, preventing European companies from helping Russia build, operate or repair energy infrastructure, particularly refineries. For the first time, the restrictions would also cover electricity-related services. The maritime measures form part of a wider package targeting Russian banks, cryptocurrency platforms, payment networks and companies in third countries accused of supporting sanctions evasion. The Commission has proposed extending the transaction ban to approximately 60 Russian banks and removing them from the SWIFT financial messaging system. A Crypto Sanctions Task Force has also been established to support enforcement and cooperation with international partners. Additional proposals would prevent European nationals from holding positions on the governing bodies of companies in Russia and introduce new visa, sporting and cultural restrictions. “Our position is clear: we are giving Ukraine the strength to secure peace – and Russia every reason to choose it,” said Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission. The proposed sanctions require the unanimous approval of EU member states before entering into force.

Join the leading maritime news network Two established naval architecture and marine engineering firms become 100% employee owned, carrying forward the vision and values of their founders. Bristol Harbor Group, Inc. (BHGI) and The Shearer Group, Inc. (TSGI) are proud to announce that both companies are now 100% employee owned through an Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP), marking an important milestone for the two naval architecture and marine engineering firms. For Gregory W. Beers, P.E., and Cory C. Wood, who founded BHGI in 1995 and later established TSGI in 2010, the transition represents the continuation of a vision that began more than three decades ago: to build the most well-respected naval architecture and marine engineering firms in the industry. Gregory and Cory have spent decades building BHGI and TSGI with a vision that extends well beyond their own leadership. Through careful planning, the development of strong management teams, and a continued investment in their employees, they have positioned both firms to become multigenerational leaders in the naval architecture and marine engineering industry. The transition to employee ownership is a significant step in securing that future, ensuring that the companies they founded continue to grow and succeed for generations to come. While ownership has changed, both firms will continue operating much as they have for years. Gregory and Cory will remain at the forefront of both companies, providing leadership and direction alongside their established management teams. Clients can continue to expect the same level of service and technical expertise from the employees they’ve come to know and trust over the years. BHGI’s History BHGI traces its origins back to 1993, when Gregory and Cory, along with Andy Tyska of Bristol Marine and another fellow student at the University of Michigan Naval Architecture and Marine Engineering Department set out to design a passenger vessel while still in school. Their first design, the STAR OF SAUGATUCK II , marked an early milestone for the firm and is still operating on the Kalamazoo River in Southwest Michigan. Building on that early initiative, the group formally incorporated BHGI in 1995, and the firm has continued to grow in Bristol, Rhode Island, ever since. Over the years, BHGI has developed into a close-knit team of 19, maintaining a hands-on, collaborative working environment. Today, the engineering team is led by Daniel P. Eling, P.E. For more than three decades, BHGI has been guided by a set of core values established early on by Greg and Cory. Those values continue to shape the firm’s work today and center on technical excellence, attention to detail, a strong focus on clients, engineering ethics, professionalism, and responsibility. TSGI’s History In 2010, Gregory and Cory formed The Shearer Group, Inc. (TSGI), a sister company to BHGI located in Houston, Texas. The company was established when Gregory and Cory purchased the assets of Shearer & Assoc., Inc. from Edward L. Shearer, P.E., its founder and president. The three had heard of one another through industry connections and eventually met at a SNAME convention. That encounter led to further discussions, and ultimately the formation of TSGI. The “Shearer” name has long been associated with the inland marine industry, reflecting both Ed’s contributions to naval architecture and his family’s multigenerational barge line. When TSGI was established, it brought together Ed’s years of experience at Shearer & Associates, Inc. and the naval architecture and marine engineering expertise Gregory and Cory had developed at BHGI. Ed remains involved as a Principal Naval Architect. Today, TSGI provides marine engineering services to clients in the inland and offshore marine industries. The firm offers many of the same services as BHGI, along with additional services suited to its Houston location, including marine surveying and OSHA-compliant maritime gear certification support. As TSGI continued to grow, Joshua S. Sebastian, P.E., joined the firm in 2013, bringing five years of engineering experience at BHGI, along with his nine-year background as an officer in the U.S. Coast Guard. He relocated to Texas to serve as Engineering Manager, as part of Gregory and Cory’s plan to build TSGI with the same technical and cultural approach used at BHGI. In 2022, Joshua stepped into the role of Vice President – Operations, with Senior Naval Architect Harrison C. Brann, P.E., stepping into the role of Engineering Manager. Over 15 years, TSGI has grown into another close-knit team of 19. Under Joshua and Harrison’s leadership, TSGI has continued to grow while maintaining the same approach and core principles established at BHGI. Today, the firm remains dedicated to serving vessels that operate on the inland waterways and continuing the tradition established by its namesake. Leadership and Employee Ownership With the ESOP now in place, Gregory will serve as Chairman and President, Cory as Vice Chairman, and Joshua as Vice President of both BHGI and TSGI. The engineering teams will continue under the direction of Daniel at BHGI and Harrison at TSGI, both as Engineering Managers. What began as a design effort in a college house has grown into two established firms, each built in a steady and deliberate way. Over the years, Gregory and Cory have built management teams that allow BHGI and TSGI to grow without losing sight of the values on which they were founded. Now, with ownership in the hands of their employees, both firms will continue the work they were built to do, guided by the same commitment to their clients, their profession, and a shared belief that their purpose is to create. To mark the transition to employee ownership, BHGI and TSGI recognized employees who were with the firms at the time as “Plank Owners,” a nautical term traditionally used for members of a vessel’s commissioning crew. Each employee received a commemorative “Built to Last” challenge coin featuring the “Plank Owner” designation. Both offices also have permanent “Plank Owner” plaques on display, recognizing these employees and their place in the companies’ history. For BHGI and TSGI, employee ownership is another part of what it means to be built to last. About BHGI Bristol Harbor Group, Inc. (BHGI) is a naval architecture and marine engineering firm located in Bristol, Rhode Island. Founded in 1995, BHGI provides vessel design, engineering, and consulting services to commercial and government clients throughout the marine industry. To learn more, you can visit our website: http://bristolharborgroup.com . About TSGI The Shearer Group, Inc. (TSGI) is a naval architecture and marine engineering firm located in Houston, Texas. Established in 2010, TSGI provides naval architecture, marine engineering, marine surveying, and related consulting services to clients in the inland and offshore marine industries. November 24, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Peter Hermes Furian Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy confirmed his country was responsible for Saturday's drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland, while Norway, a strong supporter of Kyiv, urged it to exercise caution in such operations. Finnish, Estonian and Russian vessels took part in a joint rescue operation to put out the fire. On Sunday, a Russian vessel towed the ship back into Russian waters, where it is now anchored in St Petersburg. Zelenskiy said the operation had struck a legitimate military target. "We did everything right," Zelenskiy told Bloomberg on Monday. "Every vessel with a Russian flag, everything that carries weapons or any sanctioned cargo that can carry God knows what, it is a legitimate target for us in Russian territorial or neutral waters." The Sparta II is a Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Oboronlogistika, a Russian shipping company providing logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, according to the company's website. Zelenskiy said the attack occurred in Russian territorial waters. "We had all the rights for that and then some drift happened and surely there are questions," he said. He acknowledged that some European allies were "worried when something is happening in the Baltic Sea" and said he had instructed his ministers and the military to "communicate more with partners so that they have enough details and there are no surprises". 'NEED FOR STABILITY IN OUR NEAR AREAS' Norwegian Defence Minister Tore Sandvik said on Tuesday there was an ongoing dialogue with Ukraine regarding "a need for stability in our near areas". "All attacks would stop immediately if Russia stopped this war. That said, we are focused on the fact that Ukraine must do this (these actions) within the rules of international law. So we take this matter up with them," Sandvik told reporters. "We are also focused on the fact that they must respect our need for stability in our near areas and we have a good dialogue with the Ukrainians on that now," he added. Sandvik was speaking after signing an agreement with his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, to expand bilateral cooperation on an anti-drone system in order to increase its use in more parts of Ukraine. Russian forces have been subjecting Kyiv and other cities to virtually continuous air attacks since September. Sandvik did not say whether he had discussed the Gulf of Finland attack with Khmara at their meeting. NATO member Norway has set up a long-term funding plan for Ukraine, with the backing of all parties in parliament, amounting to some $27 billion between 2023 and 2030, making it one of Kyiv's most generous backers per capita. articles.title: Maersk and ONE Eye Landmark Global North-South Shipping Alliance
articles.summary: The formation of container shipping’s first global liner alliance covering the north-south trades appears to be taking shape, The Loadstar has learned.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Containers are seen on the Maersk's Triple-E giant container ship Majestic Maersk, one of the world's largest container ships, next to cranes at the APM Terminals in the port of Algeciras, Spain January 20, 2023. REUTERS/Jon Nazca/File Photo By Nils Roche (The Loadstar) – The formation of container shipping’s first global liner alliance covering the north-south trades appears to be taking shape, The Loadstar has learned. Container lines have traditionally treated the north-south trades as a set of separate marriages, on the assumption that the right partner depends on the trade. However, according to sources in Asia, Maersk and Ocean Network Express (ONE) are working to develop a vessel-sharing agreement (VSA) covering the trades globally, rather than lane by lane. The Loadstar has approached both carriers for comment but has yet to receive a formal response, and the form the VDSA would take is unclear. Nonetheless, if confirmed it would be the first VSA of its kind – and its logic rests on ONE’s fleet, according to our provisional analysis below. Their respective groupings, the Gemini Cooperation for Maersk and Premier Alliance for ONE, stop at east-west trades, while north-south has remained a patchwork of classic VSAs, where each carrier’s slots follow the ships it provides, and an agreement rarely covers more than two or three services. Why not Hapag-Lloyd? The obvious choice of partner for Maersk would be Hapag-Lloyd, its Gemini compatriot – but two things rule it out. The first is that CSAV owns 30% of it and sits in the shareholder pact that controls more than 70% of the carrier, so combining West Coast South America networks would join two incumbents serving the same Chilean and Peruvian exporters. In that context, it is worth noting that Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd do not cooperate on any of their respective Asia-WC South America services – according to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, Maersk operates two standalone strings, the AC1 and AC3, while Hapag-Lloyd’s three offerings are run in cooperation with MSC, HMM, and ONE. Secondly, Hapag-Lloyd has relatively few ships coming – its orderbook is 19% of its fleet, the lowest of the eight largest carriers, on trades where Far East–Latin America capacity grew 14% in a year. ONE poses fewer of those problems. On Far East–WC South America, for example, Linerlytica puts Maersk at 16.1% of weekly capacity and ONE at 9%; together a quarter of the trade, ahead of CMA CGM and MSC, from two carriers whose customers overlap less. The ships are the point ONE has the fleet those trades are moving towards. Alphaliner puts 36% of its operated capacity in ships of 10,000–15,100 teu, against 14% at Maersk. Of the 55 ships ONE has on order, 29 – representing 60% of the total 647,000 teu expected – fall in the same bracket. Linerlytica puts the average ship on Far East–Latin America already at 10,032 teu. However, only 10 of ONE’s 62 ships in that class currently work Latin American routes. Under the classic formula, ships buy slots, so tonnage converts directly into share. A global partner gives ONE’s newbuilds work without ONE building Latin American and African franchises alone. Maersk, whose next order according to Linerlytica is for 24,000 teu ships, would thus get mid-size capacity without ordering it. What it will probably look like “Global” may describe the scope more than the mechanics. North-south shippers pay for direct calls, Brazil reserves feeder legs for Brazilian-flag operators, and Mexico’s ports do little relay business. That points to core loops on one carrier’s ships where its fleet fits, and shared loops where the ship mix demands it, rather than a Gemini-style hub network. The obstacles are real. Hapag-Lloyd sits alongside ONE in several of these consortia, so the deal means reordering them with Maersk’s own Gemini partner, and a quarter of Asia–WC South America capacity will interest regulators in Chile and Peru. And similar disentanglements will be necessary on other north-south trades: for example, Maersk continues to cooperate with CMA CGM on Asia-West Africa services. And although there were rumours that that cooperation might be coming to an end, they have subsided for now. The quay question… …will be where ONE’s 13,724 teu newbuilds are deployed in 2027. The industry has assumed north-south partners must be chosen trade by trade. A Maersk–ONE framework tests a different premise: that the scarce input is the right ship, and a carrier holding them can be a partner almost everywhere. articles.summary: The state-owned Shipping Corporation of India (SCI) is seeking to acquire up to 22 new vessels in a multibillion-dollar fleet expansion that could provide a major boost to India’s domestic...

Photo courtesy HD Hyundai The state-owned Shipping Corporation of India (SCI) is seeking to acquire up to 22 new vessels in a multibillion-dollar fleet expansion that could provide a major boost to India’s domestic shipbuilding industry. The procurement program spans some of the largest and most sophisticated vessels in commercial shipping, including ultra-large containerships, very large gas carriers (VLGCs) and Suezmax crude oil tankers. According to SCI’s official tender notices , the program includes eight VLGCs, six 18,000-TEU containerships, two Suezmax tankers and up to six 8,000-TEU containerships, including four optional vessels. The combined newbuilding program could be worth as much as $3.2 billion, according to India’s Economic Times. shipindia.com+2 Significantly, the tenders are structured to encourage international shipbuilders to establish manufacturing facilities in India or enter into technical partnerships with domestic shipyards. Under the VLGC tender, two vessels would be constructed at an established overseas shipyard, with the remaining six built in India. A similar arrangement calls for four of the six 18,000-TEU containerships to be constructed domestically. Indian shipyards would also receive the right of first refusal to match competing foreign bids for the smaller containerships and Suezmax tankers. Four of the six ultra-large containerships are earmarked for the proposed Bharat Container Shipping Line, part of India’s broader effort to expand its presence in global container shipping and reduce reliance on foreign carriers. SCI is separately seeking to acquire up to four secondhand containerships ranging from 1,500 to 2,500 TEU in capacity. The procurement drive comes as India pursues an ambitious goal of becoming one of the world’s five largest shipbuilding nations by 2047. The government has been courting major South Korean shipbuilders, including HD Hyundai, Samsung Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean, to invest in domestic shipbuilding capacity. Bids for the containerships and Suezmax tankers are due in December, followed by the VLGC tender in January 2027. While the vessels have yet to be ordered, the scale and structure of the procurement program underscore India’s intention to use state-backed shipping demand to develop a globally competitive shipbuilding industry. articles.title: Ex-Petrofac Executives on Trial After Alleged Bribes
articles.summary: Two former executives at British oilfield services provider Petrofac were involved in the payment of bribes to secure multibillion-dollar contracts in the United Arab Emirates, prosecutors said at the start of their trial on Tuesday.Marwan Chedid…
articles.body: Ex-Petrofac Executives on Trial After Alleged Bribes Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Lukasz Z Two former executives at British oilfield services provider Petrofac were involved in the payment of bribes to secure multibillion-dollar contracts in the United Arab Emirates, prosecutors said at the start of their trial on Tuesday. Marwan Chedid, Petrofac's former chief operating officer, and George Salibi, chief operating officer of Petrofac's engineering and construction division, are both charged with two counts of bribery which allegedly took place between 2012 and 2018 relating to the Upper Zakum offshore oilfield. Prosecutors allege the pair were involved in corrupt schemes to secure contracts worth around $3.4 billion with the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), with around $23 million in bribes paid and disguised using false invoices and third-party companies. Chedid and Salibi both pleaded not guilty ahead of their trial at London's Southwark Crown Court. Prosecutor Jonathan Kinnear said the bribes were paid through an agent called Basim Al-Shaikh, a British national who died in 2021. He added the defendants seemed to accept that payments were made but disputed that they were bribes or that they knew bribes were being paid. The first bribery charge relates to a contract to expand the capacity of the Upper Zakum oilfield to 750,000 barrels per day, with the second count relating to a variation order to increase capacity to 1 million bpd. Kinnear said bribes were paid via Al-Shaikh to other intermediaries and then on to people linked to ADNOC who were "able to assist Petrofac with their bid". Chedid and Salibi were aware of the sums paid to Al-Shaikh and there was "no legitimate or any other commercial reason for disguising the payment of money", Kinnear told the jury. "This sustained exercise of concealment is at the very heart of the case," Kinnear added. "If the defendants ... knew that payments were being made to Basim (Al-Shaikh) under the cover of false purchase orders or invoices and by way of the other underhand, indirect methods ... that is, we say, powerful evidence that they were fully aware of and participating in the offering, giving and paying of bribes." Kinnear also said that a more junior ex-Petrofac employee, David Lufkin, had previously pleaded guilty to bribery offences in relation to the Upper Zakum contracts and would give evidence for the prosecution. The trial continues and is due to conclude in March. (Reuters)

French authorities have successfully refloated the Malta-flagged bulk carrier MIRO G , four days after the vessel ran aground on France’s Atlantic coast during severe weather. The Atlantic Maritime Prefecture confirmed Tuesday afternoon that the complex salvage operation had succeeded in freeing the vessel from a beach near Lit-et-Mixe in the Landes department of southwestern France. The operation involved extensive maritime, land and aerial resources, bringing together French military personnel, government agencies and private-sector salvage specialists, including Les Abeilles International. Following the successful refloating, the French Navy deployed a Falcon 50 maritime surveillance aircraft to assess the environmental situation. No marine pollution was detected at the grounding site or along the vessel’s subsequent transit route. The MIRO G will now be taken under the care of tugs mobilized by the Port of Bordeaux for onward transit to Le Verdon, where divers will conduct an underwater inspection of the vessel’s hull to assess any damage. The successful operation follows several days of intensive preparations , including the assembly of a 1,900-meter high-strength synthetic towline aboard the French emergency towing vessel Abeille Bretagne and efforts to restore the grounded ship’s ballast pumping capabilities to reduce its draft. ?? Nineteen of its 22 crew members were subsequently evacuated by helicopter, while the captain and two crew members remained aboard to assist authorities. The 2011-built, approximately 28,200-dwt bulk carrier was sailing without cargo at the time of the incident. French maritime authorities praised the coordination and professionalism of the military and civilian teams involved in the operation, which was completed safely and without any detected pollution. articles.body: Oil Prices Rise on Hormuz Vessel Attacks Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 © Adobe Stock/le Oil prices edged higher on Tuesday in a choppy session as new attacks were reported on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, but gains were capped by an outlook for surplus global supplies. Brent crude futures bounced off a session trough that was their lowest since August 27 and were up 45 cents, or 0.5%, to $89.82 a barrel at 11:25 a.m. EDT (1625 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up 42 cents, or 0.52%, at $80.59 a barrel. Their session low was the weakest since August 10. Brent's session low was $88.10 a barrel, while WTI slipped as low as $79.07, pressured by a stock market slide. On Monday, three vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles as they sailed east through the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Tuesday. All three vessels continued their journeys and all crew members were accounted for, UKMTO said. "Expectations for excess supply continue to restrain the recovery, leaving crude sensitive to whether further attacks actually interrupt deliveries," Gelber & Associates analysts said in a note. The US is investigating whether Iran was involved in cyberattacks on as many as 50 energy tankers, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter. SUPPLY SIGNALS Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has reopened after an "unlawful group" closed a valve on the pipeline, and oil has begun to flow into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, the chairperson of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Monday. China and India are on track for record Russian oil imports this year, plugging a supply gap caused by the Iran war, according to tanker data and industry insiders. Temporary US waivers on Russian oil sanctions widened the pool of vessels and suppliers available to India and China, allowing them to increase purchases at a time when supplies from the Middle East are disrupted. But sustained Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure tempered available supplies. Russia will "inevitably" respond to the continuing Ukrainian attacks on its refineries, President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday, adding he wanted the government to discuss additional security measures for energy facilities. Putin noted that US President Donald Trump had explicitly asked Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries. The overall global oil supply outlook still was seen as a surplus. Deutsche Bank said that global observed liquids inventories rose in October, implying an oversupply of 1.7 million barrels per day. Evidence is accumulating that the global market is rebalancing and turning into surplus, although setbacks could delay progress, the bank said in a research report. US crude oil and product inventories likely rose last week, a preliminary Reuters poll showed. "Oil prices are facing modest downward pressure from two sides: markets are pricing out some near-term geopolitical risk in the Middle East, while releases from strategic reserves are keeping supply relatively comfortable despite lower regional exports and stronger Chinese demand," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo. Elsewhere, Iraq's prime minister has ordered the federal oil ministry to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish security control, the state news agency said on Tuesday, potentially deepening tensions between Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region. (Reuters)

articles.summary: Four more commercial vessels have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz, bringing the number of reported tanker strikes in the strategic waterway to 10 in a single...

REUTERS/Stringer Four more commercial vessels have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz, bringing the number of reported tanker strikes in the strategic waterway to 10 in a single week, as Iran expands its crackdown to maritime service providers assisting vessels it deems non-compliant. The latest warnings from United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) detail attacks against three tankers and a bulk carrier on November 22, underscoring the persistent threat to commercial shipping nearly nine months into the Iran war. The three tankers were struck by unidentified projectiles while transiting eastbound through the Strait of Hormuz. All three vessels continued their voyages, with all crew members accounted for. The extent of damage and any environmental impact remain unknown. UKMTO initially reported the tanker strikes under a single warning before reclassifying them as three separate attacks. In a separate incident, a bulk carrier at anchor off Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, was struck by an unidentified projectile, triggering an onboard fire. No casualties were reported. The identities of the four vessels have not been disclosed. The latest attacks follow a sustained series of strikes against outbound tankers near Oman’s Musandam Peninsula. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), in its November 22 advisory, reported that seven tankers had been struck in the Strait of Hormuz since November 16. The three subsequently reported tanker attacks bring that tally to 10. Among the earlier incidents were attacks against the tankers Torkel and Arina on November 21. JMIC continues to assess the maritime threat level in the Strait of Hormuz as severe, warning that further deliberate attacks are highly likely. Iranian claims that tankers have been struck by mines have not been independently confirmed. Iran Widens Shipping Blacklist to Tugs Meanwhile, Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) announced that it had added 26 tugboats to its list of non-compliant vessels, accusing them of providing services to ships operating in violation of its restrictions in the southern Strait of Hormuz. The authority said the tugboats had been identified through intelligence monitoring and reports from citizens in Iran’s southern neighboring countries, reiterating that vessels and companies assisting ships deemed non-compliant would themselves face blacklisting. According to maritime security analyst Martin Kelly of Orbital Risk Intelligence, Iran’s non-compliance list already contained 240 vessels as of November 19, potentially bringing the total to 266 with the latest additions. The move signals a widening of Tehran’s efforts to exert control over commercial shipping, and raises particular concerns for towing and salvage operators at a time when repeated attacks have left a growing number of vessels damaged or disabled. In its November 20 assessment, Orbital warned that further Iranian attacks on merchant vessels were highly likely over the following week, while prospects for a U.S.-Iran agreement that would end attacks on shipping remained slim. The firm also said it had seen no evidence to substantiate repeated Iranian claims that tankers had struck naval mines in the Strait. IMO Confirms 141 Incidents, 25 Seafarer Deaths The latest attacks come as the International Maritime Organization’s tally of confirmed maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and wider Middle East reached 141 as of November 23, with 25 confirmed seafarer fatalities. Among the latest vessels identified by the IMO are Captain Leon , Bahra and On Phoenix , all of which suffered damage in incidents near Oman in recent days. The four vessels involved in Sunday’s attacks have yet to appear individually on the IMO’s published list, and it remains unclear whether the latest attacks are already reflected in the organization’s cumulative tally. Hormuz Traffic Remains Depressed Despite an increase in U.S.-facilitated transits in recent days, commercial shipping activity through the Strait of Hormuz remains well below pre-war levels. According to JMIC, 114 vessels completed U.S.-facilitated transits between November 19 and 21, averaging 38 per day, up from 27 per day during the preceding four days. That compares with a historical average of approximately 138 daily vessel transits in 2025. Separately, commercial vessel tracking recorded no AIS-visible transits by qualifying cargo-carrying vessels outside the U.S.-facilitated traffic figures during the three-day period, although the data excludes certain Iranian port traffic. Approximately 218 commercial vessels remained stationary at major anchorages east of the Strait as of November 22, with JMIC expecting the backlog to persist. The renewed attacks and Iran’s widening crackdown highlight the continuing challenges facing efforts to restore commercial navigation through the world’s most important oil shipping chokepoint, even as the United States continues to facilitate vessel passages and enforce its blockade of Iranian ports. articles.title: OPEC+ Faces Its Most Consequential Supply Decision of the Year
articles.summary: When OPEC+ oil ministers gather at the end of this month to figure out how much crude to supply the world, they’ll face their most consequential decision of the year.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The Soho Square, a crude oil tanker sailing under the flag of Liberia, is at anchor in the Galveston Bay as it makes it’s way to the Port of Houston shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a 60-day waiver of the Jones Act shipping law, in Texas City, Texas, U.S. March 18, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian By Grant Smith, Nayla Razzouk and Salma El Wardany (Bloomberg) — When OPEC + oil ministers gather at the end of this month to figure out how much crude to supply the world, they’ll face their most consequential decision of the year. Saudi Arabia and its partners must plot a course for 2027, positioning themselves for the potential end of the Iran war while contending with strains inside the alliance. The United Arab Emirates has already quit after years of frustration with its production limits and Iraq has pushed for room to pump more. Integral to the talks, ministers will have to digest the results of the most comprehensive external review yet of how much each member is capable of producing, a highly sensitive exercise whose findings have so far been kept closely guarded even within OPEC+. The review, completed this month by Dallas-based consultants DeGolyer and MacNaughton Corp., seeks to put an independent number on one of the most contentious questions inside the alliance: each country’s maximum sustainable oil production capacity. Those numbers matter because they will form a new starting point for countries’ future production targets. In simple terms, the greater the capacity assigned to a country, the stronger its claim to be allowed to pump more. Yet even after the exercise concluded, members weren’t given the full picture. Countries received their own results, while OPEC+ didn’t circulate a list showing the capacity assigned to every member, according to delegates. That leaves governments heading into the meeting without knowing precisely how their capabilities stack up against their peers. The meeting of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies comes at a time of extraordinary uncertainty in the market: Will the world pump more barrels of oil each day next year than it consumes, as organizations like the International Energy Agency predict? Will rivals such as the US and Guyana keep ramping up? Will demand hold up — or even snap back — in 2027 if the war is resolved? And will consumer governments seek to replenish stockpiles heavily depleted by the conflict? “OPEC+ faces an extremely difficult call for 2027,” said Jorge Leon, head of geopolitical analysis at Rystad Energy who previously worked at the OPEC secretariat. “The group has to plan around huge uncertainty over the US-Iran war, the pace of recovery through the Strait of Hormuz, and the size of the surplus that could emerge once disrupted barrels return.” The most immediate stakes are oil prices. Brent futures have tumbled almost 25% this month as the Saudis and other Persian Gulf exporters managed to shift barrels out of the region at pre-war rates despite the ongoing hostilities. Physical markets look comfortably supplied and a renewed surplus next year could erode revenues for the petro-states that compose OPEC+. While Sunday’s meeting will be consequential for the group’s overall production policy for 2027, the impact on the short-term supply of oil will probably be more modest. Despite this month’s plunge, prices are still up by about 40% compared with a year earlier, meaning there’s no clear oil price imperative to adjust output quotas meaningfully. And even if some countries were to be assigned large new production ceilings during the audit, it’s unlikely OPEC+ will be pushing to release extra barrels onto the market. In the run-up to the meeting, Riyadh and Baghdad both said their output had recovered from wartime losses to levels that exceeded their agreed OPEC+ quotas. Before that, war-related disruption in Hormuz had forced Gulf nations to shutter output and rendered OPEC+ quotas something of a paper exercise. If the conflict flares anew, any quotas could once again become superfluous. But if the recent recovery in traffic endures, the numbers will become increasingly relevant. In addition to the uncertainties gripping the market, the audit will add an extra layer of complexity to Sunday’s decision-making process. On Nov. 16, officials from OPEC’s secretariat in Vienna and representatives from several countries held an online session to mark the conclusion of the DeGolyer and MacNaughton audit, and nations received their own results. These figures are to be used as the “baselines,” or starting points, for new production targets taking effect in January, though exactly how the new quotas will be calculated remains unclear, delegates said. They asked not to be identified as the process is private. One delegate said the Nov. 16 meeting was short and didn’t give members much opportunity to debate the new capacity levels. They said they were surprised that the group didn’t share a list of every country’s new capacity figures. OPEC’s secretariat in Vienna didn’t respond to a request for comment. Between April 2025 and September 2026, a subgroup of OPEC+ members has formally restored two layers of output halted in 2023 through a series of monthly quota increases, which continued even when the Iran war rendered the hikes symbolic. That process still technically leaves offline a third tranche of output that was idled back in 2022, though factoring this into new targets for 2027 is further complicated by the deterioration of output capacity many members have experienced in the meantime, owing to issues like under-investment and sanctions. In practice, the capacity review may ultimately allow only a handful of countries to boost production. Many members are already close to their limits, while others — most notably Saudi Arabia — are expected to retain spare capacity. The country that has most intensely lobbied for a higher baseline, and the right to pump more, is Iraq. In June, the nation’s oil ministry briefly warned it could decide “whether to remain in or withdraw” from the organization — founded in Baghdad more than six decades ago — if the results of its capacity assessment weren’t high enough. While the country subsequently withdrew the threat, Baghdad has chafed for years at OPEC quotas while it seeks to rebuild its shattered economy. Baghdad is seeking a production baseline of 6 million barrels a day, people familiar with the matter said in September. The warning carried extra weight because it came just weeks after the UAE announced its departure from the group after decades of stalwart membership, citing frustrations with limits on deploying supplies from new oil projects. Abu Dhabi’s production has subsequently reached new records of more than 5 million barrels a day, according to the IEA. Previous reviews of how much members can pump have proved contentious. An assessment of Angola’s capacity in 2023 spurred the country to quit OPEC after 16 years of membership. Ultimately, though, the fate of the war — rather than the outcome of the audit — may have the biggest influence of all on how much oil OPEC nations end up pumping in the coming year. Oil flows have held up in recent weeks, despite a surge in attacks by Iran on vessels going through Hormuz. At the same time, the US is maintaining a strict blockade on Iran’s shipping, pressuring Tehran. “Given Iran’s stated objective to break the blockade by any means necessary, the actual live fire in the region could still be more consequential in the near term than any rhetorical fireworks over production targets even with the recent rise in Hormuz transits,” said Helima Croft, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Designed to deliver power at the point of need, Kratos is a modular energy system developed for operations where conventional infrastructure may be unavailable, compromised or denied. By unanimous vote, officers elected include Donald M. Schexnayder, West Baton Rouge Parish, as president; Rev. Shelton C. Dixon, East Baton Rouge Parish, as vice president; Ted H. Glaser, Pointe Coupee Parish, as secretary; and Johnny B. Bradberry, East Baton Rouge Parish as treasurer. Donald M. Schexnayder , president, is a lifelong Louisiana agricultural leader, landowner, and public servant with more than three decades of experience in farming, conservation, and economic development. He is a partner and owner-operator of Schexnayder Planting and Manufacturing and serves as owner/operator of R. Schexnayder & Sons, LLC. Mr. Schenayder has long been active in agricultural advocacy and conservation leadership. He has served as president of the West Baton Rouge Farm Bureau Board since 2019 and as Louisiana Farm Bureau State Chairman of the Soybeans, Wheat and Feed Grain Committee for more than 15 years. He has also served for more than 25 years as a commissioner of the Upper Delta Soil and Water Conservation District and has been a board member of the Louisiana Landowners Association since 2020. In addition to his agricultural work, Mr. Schexnayder has played a significant role in regional economic development through his service on the Greater Baton Rouge Port Commission since 1998. Rev. Shelton C. Dixon , vice president, is the organizer and pastor of Greater Mount Olive Missionary Baptist Church in Baton Rouge, which he founded in 1996. He currently serves as General Secretary of the National Baptist Convention of America International, Inc. and since October 2019 has been serving as General President of the Louisiana Home and Foreign Missions Baptist Convention. Rev. Dixon was appointed to the Greater Baton Rouge Port Commission in 2020. His service to the community includes leadership roles with numerous civic and faith-based organizations. He also serves as a board member on the Louisiana Board of Embalmers and Funeral Directors. Ted H. Glaser , secretary, is a longtime Louisiana farmer and respected agricultural leader. He and his son, Abram, operate Glaser Farms Partnership in Pointe Coupee Parish, established in 1980, where they primarily produce sugarcane. Over the years, Mr. Glaser has held numerous leadership roles within the agricultural community, including serving as First Vice President of the Louisiana Farm Bureau and as a board member for Southern Farm Bureau Casualty Company and Farm Bureau Mutual Insurance Company. In recognition of his contributions to the industry, he was named Louisiana Farmer of the Year in 2000. His public service includes work with the USDA County Committee, Tri-Parish Cotton Gin, and the Louisiana Farm Bureau Marketing Board. He remains actively engaged in both his local community and the state through his service on the Louisiana Board of Regents and the Greater Baton Rouge Port Commission. Johnny B. Bradberry , treasurer, serves as President of G.E.C., Inc. (GEC), where he leads the engineering firm's strategic direction, operational performance, business development, and long-term growth initiatives. With more than 50 years of experience across engineering, public service, transportation, coastal restoration, oil and gas, and industrial development, he brings extensive leadership experience and a broad understanding of complex infrastructure and environmental challenges. Prior to joining GEC, Mr. Bradberry served as Executive Assistant to the Governor for Coastal Activities and Chairman of the Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, helping guide implementation of Louisiana's Coastal Master Plan. He also served as Secretary of the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development, overseeing statewide transportation programs and infrastructure investments. His career includes 28 years in the upstream and midstream oil and gas industry, as well as executive leadership roles with TOPCOR Companies and Volkert, Inc. He has served on the Port of Greater Baton Rouge Port Commission since 2024. The Port Commission is a 17-member governing body appointed by the Governor of Louisiana to establish policy and provide oversight for the port's development. Commissioners represent the five parishes served by the port: Ascension, Iberville, East Baton Rouge, West Baton Rouge and Pointe Coupee. Elections for new officers are held annually.

REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo Marine insurer The Swedish Club is warning shipowners against non-essential transits of the Strait of Hormuz as escalating attacks on commercial shipping, mounting congestion and persistent navigational interference further deteriorate the security environment in the Middle East. In an operational update issued Tuesday, the Gothenburg-based P&I club reaffirmed its recommendation that members avoid the strategic waterway unless passage is operationally essential. The warning follows a fresh wave of attacks on merchant vessels, particularly tankers navigating waters off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula. The warning comes as the International Maritime Organization (IMO) raised its tally of confirmed maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and wider Middle East to 141 as of November 23, with 25 seafarers confirmed dead. The latest additions include three vessels damaged off Oman between November 17 and 20. The actual scale of the crisis could be considerably greater. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) had already recorded 181 regional security incidents as of November 12, although the two organizations apply different reporting and verification criteria. Despite ongoing U.S.-facilitated transits, commercial shipping activity through Hormuz remains well below prewar levels. Independent monitoring cited by the Club recorded just 106 facilitated transits between November 15 and 18, averaging 26.5 vessels per day. The insurer also warned that ships accumulating at anchorages east of the Strait face heightened exposure to potential attacks, particularly during prolonged periods at anchor. The continuing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and Tehran’s expanding blacklist of commercial vessels have introduced additional risks for shipowners. Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority reportedly increased its list of non-compliant vessels to 240 earlier this month. The Swedish Club urged operators to reassess their war-risk insurance arrangements, sanctions exposure, navigational capabilities and crew readiness before committing to voyages through the region. Crucially, the insurer cautioned that neither the continued movement of commercial shipping nor previous successful passages should be interpreted as assurances of safe transit. The advisory underscores the widening disconnect between efforts to restore commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and the security risks that merchant ships and their crews continue to face on a daily basis. articles.title: Used Supertankers Now Cost More Than New Ships as Hormuz War Upends Shipping Markets
articles.summary: The war with Iran has so severely distorted the global oil tanker market that 15-year-old supertankers are now worth considerably more than brand-new vessels, highlighting the extraordinary premium placed on...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche The war with Iran has so severely distorted the global oil tanker market that 15-year-old supertankers are now worth considerably more than brand-new vessels, highlighting the extraordinary premium placed on immediately available shipping capacity. Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH revealed Tuesday in its third-quarter earnings report that the market value of a 15-year-old very large crude carrier (VLCC) has reached $165 million, some 25% above the $132 million price of ordering a new vessel, according to Clarksons data. The valuation is more than three-and-a-half times the 10-year average of $46 million for a tanker of that age. While newbuildings ordered today may take years to deliver, existing vessels can immediately capitalize on some of the highest tanker freight rates ever recorded. The unusual price inversion underscores how the war has fundamentally altered the economics of moving oil out of the Middle East. A Growing Capacity Crunch Although Middle Eastern oil exports have recovered substantially since the early months of the conflict, the shipping industry is relying on increasingly inefficient arrangements to move crude through the Strait of Hormuz. Combined oil exports from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Qatar reached 10.9 million barrels per day in October, up from 6.7 million barrels per day in April. However, much of that recovery has been facilitated by shuttle voyages and ship-to-ship transfers in the relatively safer waters of the Gulf of Oman. CMB.TECH estimates that 141 tankers are now dedicated exclusively to shuttling crude and petroleum products, with VLCCs accounting for 72% of those vessels. However, according to the CMB.TECH, the number of vessels deployed for shuttling only partly explains why tanker tonnage has become so tight. “A key additional factor is waiting time, with average round voyages extending to 23 days compared with an optimal 9 to 10 days,” the company said. The arrangement effectively removes significant tanker capacity from the wider international market, even as the global fleet continues to grow. The resulting shortage has spilled into other trading regions, driving up freight rates far beyond the Middle East as charterers compete for available tonnage. Unprecedented Earnings CMB.TECH’s Euronav tanker division reported average VLCC spot earnings of $149,945 per day in the third quarter, compared with $30,486 per day a year earlier. So far in the fourth quarter, those earnings have climbed to an extraordinary $635,199 per day, with 59% of available vessel days booked. The company’s Suezmax fleet is also benefiting, securing fourth-quarter spot earnings averaging $377,164 per day, with 68% of available days booked. The booming market has prompted CMB.TECH to capitalize on soaring vessel valuations. The company reported third-quarter net profit of $373.9 million, compared with $17.3 million a year earlier, including $100.2 million in gains from the sale of two Suezmax tankers. Three additional tanker sales are expected to generate approximately $190.8 million in gains during the fourth quarter. A Growing Risk of Reversal The extraordinary market conditions are also encouraging investment in new tanker capacity. The global VLCC orderbook now stands at 33.1% of the existing fleet, while the Suezmax orderbook has reached 29.3%, according to Clarksons data presented by CMB.TECH. An eventual normalization of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could release significant tanker capacity back into the international market, potentially coinciding with a wave of newbuilding deliveries in the coming years. Until then, however, CMB.TECH expects the availability of vessels, rather than underlying oil demand, to remain the primary driver of crude tanker earnings. For now, the fact that a 15-year-old supertanker commands a $33 million premium over a new vessel illustrates just how valuable existing shipping capacity has become in a world at war. articles.title: ShipVet Appoints New CEO as Founder Steps Back
articles.summary: Marine assurance and vessel vetting company ShipVet has appointed James Stairmand as chief executive officer, effective November 2026, as founder Captain Fintan Cullen moves to a non-executive role.Stairmand, previously the company's chief commercial officer…
articles.body: ShipVet Appoints New CEO as Founder Steps Back Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 James Stairmand (Credit: ShipVet) Marine assurance and vessel vetting company ShipVet has appointed James Stairmand as chief executive officer, effective November 2026, as founder Captain Fintan Cullen moves to a non-executive role. Stairmand, previously the company's chief commercial officer, joined ShipVet as part of a management buy-in in late 2024, backed by Frontier Development Capital. Since the investment, ShipVet has expanded its vessel vetting team with specialists from major oil companies, rebuilt its digital platform and strengthened its sanctions screening capabilities. The company's platform supports vessel assessments and sanctions screening, with maritime specialists evaluating the findings against clients' vetting policies and providing recommendations. Stairmand has more than 20 years of experience in the commodities sector and previously founded, expanded and exited OnlineFuels, a digital marketplace for downstream fuels. Cullen, who founded ShipVet in 1997, will remain involved with the company as a non-executive director. Headquartered in London, ShipVet provides independent vessel vetting and marine assurance services to the oil, gas and commodities sectors, including vessel suitability assessments, vetting policy design and sanctions screening. “Charterers need to understand the risks associated with a vessel and how those risks relate to their own requirements. Our job is to provide a clear assessment and be available to discuss it. “Fintan has built a business that clients trust. Since the buy-in, we have invested in the expertise and technology needed to develop that service further. My focus as CEO is to bring it to more charterers while preserving the judgement and responsiveness that have underpinned ShipVet’s work,” said James Stairmand, Chief Executive Officer of ShipVet.

articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard has sought a specialized salvage inspection of the damaged No. 2 diesel generator aboard USCGC Healy, seeking to identify components that can be reclaimed and reused following a catastrophic engine failure.

U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard has sought a specialized salvage inspection of the damaged No. 2 diesel generator aboard USCGC Healy , seeking to identify components that can be reclaimed and reused following a catastrophic engine failure. The procurement goes well beyond a conventional engine repair contract. The Coast Guard’s October 21 statement of work calls for a comprehensive, component-by-component assessment of the damaged Sulzer 12ZAV40S engine, including measurements against allowable clearances, an evaluation of component wear and identification of parts suitable for reclamation and reuse. The contractor must document its findings in a comprehensive report with high-resolution color photographs. The Coast Guard announced its intent to award the work on a sole-source basis to Virginia-based Defense Maritime Solutions. The inspection was scheduled for October 26–30 at Coast Guard Base Seattle. The solicitation also included an optional work item, capped at $100,000, to inspect, repair and requalify the engine’s camshaft. The documents do not establish whether that option was exercised or what the inspection ultimately found. The work follows the July casualty, when Healy suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of its No. 2 main propulsion diesel generator while operating northwest of Port Angeles, Washington. The vessel was towed to Seattle on July 13. Related procurement documents describe a fire in Generator Room No. 2 that exposed fire-detection equipment and wiring to high temperatures, causing a ground fault and requiring extensive replacement work. The casualty disrupted the cutter’s planned Arctic summer deployment . The Coast Guard has also been addressing maintenance requirements on engines No. 1 and No. 3. A separate October procurement sought overhaul of their governors and overspeed protection equipment. Both governors had accumulated more than 40,000 operating hours, with no documented service or overhaul history. The work also called for replacing a damaged cylinder head on engine No. 3. The removed head and dummy valve were to be sent to a machine shop for inspection and reconditioning in accordance with original equipment manufacturer specifications. The Coast Guard specified cylinder head part number 107.122.903.200, National Stock Number 2815-01-465-2075. Separately, supply-chain database records for the part list no active suppliers and indicate that the government does not hold the technical-data rights needed to have alternative manufacturers reproduce it using the proprietary data. The database’s acquisition guidance calls for purchasing directly from the actual manufacturer. This does not establish that the part is unavailable, but it could limit alternative sourcing options if the original manufacturer cannot supply it . “Most of the machinery systems aboard are antiquated and for some there aren’t even parts,” Vice Commandant of the Coast Guard Admiral Kevin E. Lunday said previously following a fire aboard Healy in 2024. Engine challenges are not entirely new for Healy . In 2020, a fire damaged the ship’s starboard propulsion motor, forcing it to abandon an Arctic deployment . The Coast Guard replaced the motor with a spare that had been stored at the Coast Guard Yard in Baltimore for 23 years. Moving the roughly 100-ton unit to a California shipyard required a barge voyage through the Panama Canal and removal of part of the ship’s hull for installation. The latest procurement records do not establish whether the No. 2 diesel generator can be returned to service or which of its components can be recovered. They do, however, show the Coast Guard undertaking a detailed salvage assessment and highlight potential parts-sourcing challenges across the remaining propulsion plant. articles.summary: Ukraine's foreign minister said on Tuesday a drone attack against a Russian military vessel and cargo ship in Libyan waters at the weekend was a legitimate act of self-defense, following criticism from the government in Tripoli.

KYIV, Nov 24 (Reuters) – Ukraine’s foreign minister said on Tuesday a drone attack against a Russian military vessel and cargo ship in Libyan waters at the weekend was a legitimate act of self-defense, following criticism from the government in Tripoli. Andrii Sybiha said that both Russian naval vessels and cargo ships transporting military equipment were valid targets and Ukraine’s right to self-defense was enshrined in the United Nations charter, Article 51. Libya’s Tripoli-based Government of National Unity condemned on Monday the Ukrainian military operation that sank the Russian naval corvette Merkury in the eastern port of Benghazi. It said Libya would not accept being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Benghazi is controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army has ties with Russia. The internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli controls western Libya. “Ukraine is not ‘dragging’ anyone into the war or ‘transferring’ the war anywhere,” Sybiha said on the Telegram messaging app. “Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine’s actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people.” International law does not limit the right to self-defense to the territory where the aggression takes place: it can be on the territory of the aggressor, or in international waters, Sybiha said. Russia, he said, was the one endangering third countries by using their civilian infrastructure for its military purposes. The Institute for the Study of War said the Russian naval corvette had stopped over for several days at Benghazi port to refuel and resupply, under a cooperation agreement, as it escorted cargo ships that can carry military supplies to Russia. The eastern government in Benghazi on Monday said there were indications the naval drones were launched from western Libya and asked the UN to investigate allegations that Ukraine has deployed military experts there. Russia’s defense minister has not commented publicly on the attack. In an interview published on Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy confirmed that Ukraine was responsible for a separate drone strike on Saturday on a Russian cargo vessel in the international waters of the Gulf of Finland. He said the vessel, Sparta II, was a legitimate target because it was carrying weapons. The damaged vessel was towed back to the Russian port of St Petersburg, Russia’s Transport Ministry said on Tuesday.
